text:
NEW YORK -- Nearly 200 activists in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s “Make America Healthy Again” movement are criticizing President Donald Trump's promotion of coal to fuel the rise of artificial intelligence data centers, according to a letter sent Friday.

The letter, signed by at least two former staffers from Kennedy's 2024 presidential campaign, marks the first major MAHA movement mobilization over fossil fuels and the latest in a series of rifts between the diverse group of activists and the Trump administration over environmental policy.

The letter to Trump, Kennedy and various other Cabinet officials, first obtained by The Associated Press, laments a 2025 executive order that aimed to boost coal to power data centers over pollution concerns and asks the administration to consider renewable options, including solar and geothermal energy.

“We understand the importance of American leadership in artificial intelligence, national security, innovation, and economic growth,” the letter reads. “But American AI leadership should not come at the cost of a more toxic burden for American children.”

In response, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers noted that greenhouse gas emissions dropped to a 30-year low during Trump's first term and said Trump “was given a mandate to roll back the radical climate policies that are burning a hole through taxpayers' wallets.”

The agencies receiving the letter didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Prominent MAHA figures behind the letter include Zen Honeycutt, a former Kennedy campaign staffer and founder of the advocacy group Moms Across America, and Charles Eisenstein, a former speechwriter on Kennedy's campaign. Honeycutt said she asked the Kennedy-aligned political action committee MAHA Action to sign onto the letter but did not receive a reply.

Although it may not reflect the views of all MAHA activists, the new line of criticism against one of the administration’s signature policies less than three months before November’s midterm elections could present another challenge for Republicans as they seek to win over the voting bloc in key races.

As health secretary, Kennedy has carried out several policy changes that cater to the MAHA movement, including attempting to scale back childhood vaccine recommendations, a central priority for some activists. He also has sought to remove artificial dyes from food and encouraged Americans to have healthy diets free of ultraprocessed foods.

But many in the MAHA movement, which Trump credits with helping him win back the White House two years ago, say they have grown frustrated with the administration over its embrace of pesticides such as glyphosate and its deregulatory environmental agenda. Some have said they plan to vote on issues over party this fall, raising the political stakes of their increasingly public tensions with the Republican administration.

As president, Trump has enthusiastically embraced what he calls “big, beautiful coal” despite outcry from environmentalists about planet-warming greenhouse gases and toxic chemicals released by coal-fired power plants.

His administration has moved to reverse tighter Biden-era standards on greenhouse gas emissions, which, in addition to their climate impacts, can harm brain development in children and increase rates of heart attacks in adults.

He also has been a vocal advocate for data centers, which power artificial intelligence and cloud computing, framing them as a necessary component of winning the AI race against China.

“If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state, and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center,” Trump said this week, “I would absolutely want it because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous.”

Data centers have become a political flashpoint in this year's elections. Voters across the political spectrum have criticized them for jacking up electricity bills, draining water supplies, and creating unhealthy amounts of air and noise pollution.

Friday's letter asks the administration to require transparent review of data center location and power sourcing decisions, and respect existing environmental review requirements in the permitting process.

Honeycutt said that after Trump's executive order last year, she researched the impact of coal ash on communities and was disturbed by what she found. She said she was also concerned about other aspects of data centers, including their land use and their effects on the people living near them.

“The data center push has been an overwhelmingly negative impact on our communities, and there are many in the MAHA movement that are extremely disappointed about that,” she said. “We vote for those who put health and safety first.”

____

Associated Press writer Michael Phillis in Washington contributed to this report.

title: This Cheap Electric Ford Could Be The Modern-Day Mini-Truck America Forgot It Wanted
description:
The Ford Maverick set a sales record in 2025 with 155,051 pickups sold, an 18.2 percent jump over the previous year.
The $28,350 Answer Is Called The Ford Fathom Ford announced on August 6, 2026, that its new electric pickup will be called the Fathom, at a price of $28,350.
Ford Rebuilt The Assembly Line To Build The Fathom Louisville Assembly Plant went quiet in late 2025, so Ford could spend $2 billion tearing it apart.
That $2 billion is part of roughly $5 billion Ford has committed across two sites, with the remaining $3 billion going to BlueOval Battery Park Michigan.
The 2025 Lightning started near $55,000, roughly $15,000 above the number Ford floated when reservations opened in 2021, and price did most of the damage.
text:
America used to sell small, cheap pickups that did honest work without costing a fortune, and that category has all but vanished. Americans paid an average of $49,855 for a new vehicle in July 2026, with pickups the priciest segment at $66,980.

The F-Series has been America's best-selling truck for 49 straight years, but after watching the market react to the all-electric F-150 Lightning, it is hard to fathom why Ford would build another battery-powered pickup at all. One is coming anyway in 2027, priced at less than half that average truck, reviving a body style America walked away from in 1982.

The Small Truck America Started Buying Again

Kei truck exports from Japan to the United States have more than tripled over the past five years, with over 7,500 arriving in a single recent year against roughly 1,800 five years earlier, according to the Japan Used Motor Vehicle Export Association. These tiny work trucks change hands for $5,000 to $10,000 used, a fraction of what a new American pickup costs. They are street legal in 19 states under the 25-year import rule, and the buyers are mostly farmers, landscapers, contractors and delivery operators working in tight spaces.

The Ford Maverick set a sales record in 2025 with 155,051 pickups sold, an 18.2 percent jump over the previous year. Combined entry-level trim sales across the Maverick, Ranger and Bronco Sport climbed 41.3 percent in the fourth quarter alone. Ranger volume grew 53.6 percent to 70,960 units, with the base Ranger XL up 82.3 percent as buyers hunted for the cheapest way into a truck.

The Courier arrived for 1972 with a sub-2.0-liter four-cylinder, a four-speed manual, rear-wheel drive and roughly 1,400 pounds of load capacity, all for far less money than a full-size pickup. Ford shipped every one as an incomplete stake-body truck and bolted the beds on stateside, sidestepping the 25% chicken tax on imported pickups. Production ended after 1982, when the domestically built Ranger took over the segment.

Nothing in Ford's current lineup fills the slot the Courier once held at the bottom of the range. The Maverick comes closest, and it is a crossover-based unibody rather than a genuinely small work truck.

The $28,350 Answer Is Called The Ford Fathom

Ford announced on August 6, 2026, that its new electric pickup will be called the Fathom, at a price of $28,350. Destination and delivery of $1,595 brings the total to $29,945, landing under the $30,000 figure Ford had been promising for years. The truck seats five, officially claiming to offer more space in the interior than a Toyota RAV4.

The name comes from the old nautical measure taken from a man's outstretched arms, chosen to signal how much room is inside the cabin. It also means the wordplay writes itself, and Ford appears to have made peace with that.

The Maverick XL, Ford's cheapest gas truck, starts at $28,145. That puts the electric one roughly $200 above it, which is remarkable in a market where batteries have added $15,000 or more to comparable pickups. Ford has effectively priced electricity at parity with gasoline inside its own showroom.

At $29,945 out the door, the Fathom becomes the least expensive electric vehicle Ford sells, and pricing for other configurations has not been released. Preorders open in early 2027, with customer deliveries starting that fall. It arrives as a 2028 model year truck.

Ford calls the Fathom a midsize pickup, and it will carry more passenger volume than a Toyota RAV4, which is a genuinely useful yardstick for anyone cross-shopping a family crossover. Every truck gets BlueCruise capability and bidirectional power that can run tools and appliances off the battery.

Those features are what separate the Fathom from a stripped-out kei truck, and from the Courier that Ford abandoned 45 years ago. This time there is no Mazda badge hiding underneath.

Ford Rebuilt The Assembly Line To Build The Fathom

Louisville Assembly Plant went quiet in late 2025, so Ford could spend $2 billion tearing it apart. Crews unbolted heavy machinery and removed thousands of tons of steel out the doors, and by February 2026 only the shell remained. Plant manager Brian McGauley said that from the middle of the floor, "you could see all four walls."

That $2 billion is part of roughly $5 billion Ford has committed across two sites, with the remaining $3 billion going to BlueOval Battery Park Michigan. Between them, the projects create or secure nearly 4,000 jobs, including 2,200 hourly positions in Louisville.

The plant now runs Ford's Universal EV Production System, which splits the truck into a front clip, a rear clip and a battery deck. Each section gets built at the same time in a different part of the building, and the three only marry once most components are already installed.

Large aluminum unicastings make that split possible, replacing dozens of stamped and welded pieces with a single part. Because a unicasting is structurally whole on its own, it never has to be welded into a full body shell before interior work begins. Electrek reports the change cuts the front and rear structure from 146 parts on the current Maverick down to two.

Seats, consoles and carpeting install on top of the battery, which serves as the floor, and the battery itself goes in from underneath. The prismatic LFP cells contain no cobalt or nickel, which makes them cheaper and less prone to fire than conventional packs, though less energy dense.

Installing a seat on a conventional line means squeezing through a doorway and working around the structure with tools in hand, while the new process bolts it to an open rear clip. Chief manufacturing officer Bryce Currie says the layout cuts reaching over the fender by 84%, and the wiring harness runs more than 4,000 feet shorter and 22 lbs lighter than in Ford's first electric SUV.

The system builds the Fathom 40% faster than Louisville's current products, though Ford poured much of that saved time back into automation and insourcing, leaving a net gain of 15%. Prototype builds using production-qualified parts start in the first quarter of 2027.

Ford Lost Billions On Its Last Electric Pickup

The F-150 Lightning sold 15,617 units in 2022, 24,165 in 2023 and 33,510 in 2024 before slipping to roughly 24,577 through 2025, against a plant built for 150,000 a year. That gap is the reason the Fathom exists at all.

Sales collapsed once the $7,500 federal tax credit expired at the end of September 2025. Ford's EV sales fell 60.8 percent that November, and Lightning deliveries dropped 72% to a mere 1,006 trucks.

Ford ended production of the 2025 model year Lightning that December, with Ford Blue and Model e president Andrew Frick pointing to market realities and customer preferences rather than the supplier fire that had already halted the line. A gas-generator extended-range version will replace it. Ford's Model e division lost $2.2 billion in 2022, $4.7 billion in 2023, $5.1 billion in 2024 and $3.6 billion through 2025.

The 2025 Lightning started near $55,000, roughly $15,000 above the number Ford floated when reservations opened in 2021, and price did most of the damage. The Fathom is expected to land about $26,000 below that.

Slate Auto forced the issue with a $24,950 electric pickup, opening preorders in June 2026 with a base range estimate raised from 150 to around 205 miles. Every Slate leaves the line as an identical gray, single-cab, two-seat truck with no factory paint.

The Fathom is expected to include comforts the Slate will not, among them an audio system and power windows. Slate says it has taken more than 150,000 reservations, with production due in Indiana by the end of 2026.

What Ford Is Not Telling Us Yet

Battery capacity, EPA range, towing capacity and payload ratings are all still blank, and Ford says those numbers arrive alongside the preorder announcement. The production exterior has not been shown either, so every rendering circulating online is guesswork.

Ford has promised a 0-60 mph time under 4.5 seconds and a 400-volt architecture, and the longer-range version should clear 290 miles. The $7,500 federal EV credit disappeared under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on September 30, 2025, so the $28,350 price has to stand on its own.

What Ford has confirmed is a truck with a bed, a frunk and a cabin with more space than a RAV4 for the price of a base Maverick, which is the closest anyone has come to a modern Courier since 1982.

title: A year in, the data center/AI battle starts to clarify
description:
According to a new poll from Heatmap, 75 percent of Americans oppose data center development near them.
One way to view a data center is as a machine to burn huge quantities of natural gas—which in turn is one reason why the oil-soaked Trump administration likes them so much.
The data center buildout is the work of the biggest companies in America, controlled by the most callow human beings.
Three—Its’s clear by now that AI, and the data center development underlying it, pose real and significant dangers.
“There are few feelings worse than escaping the extreme summer heat only to find yourself on a subway platform that is even hotter,” Mayor Mamdani said.
text:
One of the year’s most important political battles—the one against ICE deportations in Minneapolis this past winter—took place in a geographically confined area filled with people with cellphones who could record its brutal but fairly simple dynamic. The other—the fight against data centers—is sprawling and nationwide, often taking place in rural areas where journalism is all but nonexistent, and has generated few dramatic images beyond people yelling at county board meetings. It’s been very effective—earlier this month even Texas governor Greg Abbott, facing a tough re-election fight, called for an “audit” and temporary freeze on new connections. According to a new poll from Heatmap, 75 percent of Americans oppose data center development near them. But the opposition has also been hard to parse. There are few nationally recognizable names leading the battle, no single book or documentary guiding the fight.

I’ve had a front row seat for parts of it, because my Third Act colleagues across the country have been avid participants in many of the fights (we’re hosting a big webinar next week, in fact) and even so I’ve found it hard to really keep track of. But we’re about a year in to the most heated part of the battle, and I think we can say a few things with assurance. And a few things with less assurance. So here we go, in descending order of confidence.

One—It really is an environmental plague. Those impacts look different in different places; in dry areas, for instance, the use of water is egregious, and its effect on electric rates will vary from one jurisdiction to another. But for those who are concerned about the rapid warming of the planet, the last few weeks have made it finally clear that there’s an unholy alliance between Big Tech and Big Fossil. Many thanks to Bloomberg’s New Energy team for a comprehensive breakdown showing that the planned data center buildout will increase greenhouse gas emissions from the electricity sector by at least twenty percent, and perhaps as much as a third. That’s because—in their effort to go fast, and bypass as much permitting as possible—data center developers are increasingly opting to run them with what Matt Day and Mark Chediak called “bespoke” gas power plants. To give you a sense of the scale, here’s a couple of projects in Texas:

Earlier this month, Cleanview, which tracks US power infrastructure and data center development, identified Amazon as the developer of an 8,000-acre site in Pecos County, which will become among the biggest single sources of carbon pollution in the US.

About 30 miles (48 kilometers) to the west, past a pecan orchard and scrublands dotted with oil derricks, Chevron Corp. is building Microsoft a gas plant to power a new data center complex on a 2,000-acre site.

The two plants alone could generate more than 10 gigawatts of electricity, enough to power New York City on a hot summer day. Their combined annual emissions may be as high as 45 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to regulatory filings. That’s slightly less than half the cumulative emissions of Washington state, where both companies are headquartered.

In Ohio, as Kalley Kwang reported last week, Open AI and Nvidia are at work on a vast data center that will cost as much as half a trillion dollars and consume

eight gigawatts of computing capacity, or enough electricity to power about six million households in the United States.

One way to view a data center is as a machine to burn huge quantities of natural gas—which in turn is one reason why the oil-soaked Trump administration likes them so much. Indeed, earlier this month the president said that “data centers could be bigger than oil.” This comes at precisely the wrong moment, just when clean energy is offering us a chance to blunt the worst impacts of rapidly rising temperatures. California has managed to cut its use of natural gas for electricity in half in the last three years by building solar panels; that great gain would be wiped out by this sudden bloom of archaic gas technology.

Two—It’s clear by now that this is all part of the extension of oligarchic control over our lives. The data center buildout is the work of the biggest companies in America, controlled by the most callow human beings. Elon Musk fuels his weird and racist Grok AI by running huge diesel engines day and night in poor and Black neighborhoods to Tennessee and Mississippi; Meta is building out the biggest of the Texas plants in service of Mark “Pervert Glasses” Zuckerberg’s vision of a “personal superintelligence” “that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about.” Jeff Bezos’ Amazon is intent on a new Texas data center that Hiroko Tabuchi has reported may be the single most polluting facility in the entire country.

A few years ago these men were still held in some esteem. Not so now; they’re seen, rightly, as people whose own greed drives them. Another way of thinking about AI is as an IPO waiting to happen. These barons lined up behind President Trump on inauguration day (and Musk in particular got him the job); they get to share the rising hatred of the president.

Three—Its’s clear by now that AI, and the data center development underlying it, pose real and significant dangers. One is economic; what economic growth the Trump administration has managed to generate is focused in this sector, and it seems increasingly certain that it’s a bubble that will burst with real economic consequences. As the indefatigable journalist/gadfly Ed Zitron has been pointing out repeatedly, the revenues from large language models seem unlikely to equal the vast sums paid out to build the data centers; each day is a test to see whether the stock markets (and hence people’s retirement accounts) defy gravity a little longer.

But there’s a much deeper kind of risk from AI. I highly recommend listening to Ezra Klein’s interview with industry analyst Helen Toner earlier this week. Klein has been a (guarded) booster of AI tech, bringing knowledgeable enthusiasm for its uses. But the news in recent weeks that models from both AI and Anthropic broke the rules their programmers had set for them and figured out how to hack other companies had him talking in a new tone.

We are not out of the territory wherein we can be confident that the A.I. is not going to do something criminal and possibly catastrophic in order to solve an incredibly stupid problem.

A new industry open letter last month, signed by more than a thousand AI professionals, essentially begged the federal government to step in and impose some regulations. As they said,

The world's leading AI companies believe they could be close to automating AI research. It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate AI progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.

One of the signatories, an AI scientist at Anthropic, went further, tweeting:

Not only is AI "not guaranteed" to make a dramatically better future, the odds of failure are terrifyingly high: I think* there's something like a 40% chance we get an outcome around as bad as human extinction or worse

People intuit these risks, even if few of us really understand them.

Four—In part, that’s because the daily experience of using AI is so grim for so many people. We can acknowledge that certain forms of the technology—the machine learning that predates large language models, for instance—may help with things like medical research; for people with deep expertise in a field it can offer a (closely-watched) assist. But for most of us, day to day, this is just a new form of unwelcome harassment. Garrett Graff, the incisive journalist, used his newsletter this week to detail the many ways AI is “making everything worse.” Citing everything from the new scams it’s enabling to the much-touted hope by AI execs that it will steal millions of jobs, he concludes:

The ordinary Americans’ experience with AI is as if after the invention of electricity, every factory worker was assigned to start each workday by receiving an electric shock, and newly founded electrical companies went around to rural farms tasering farm children involuntarily and then dropping a dead electrocuted hog down the family water well.

(Which is the kind of robust sentence Claude is unlikely to produce.)

Pretty much all of us who teach are clear that it is undermining student’s ability to learn to research, and really to think; new data from China seems to show large-scale and alarming effects. Kids intuit this, and at some level resent being the guinea pigs in this vast experiment

Five—(and remember, these arguments are going by descending level of sturdiness), I think people intuit something else here. I’ve written an entire book and large parts of another trying to understand what it is about these technologies that worry me. Past the practical dangers, there’s a profound personal and even spiritual one: they’re basically about transcending the limitations of being human. But it seems increasingly clear to me that those limitations are precisely what makes being a human so interesting.

At the most basic level, much of the Silicon Valley fascination with this stuff stems from a widely-advertised fear of…dying. Ray Kurzweil, whose job at Google is “AI Visionary,” is the prophet of the Singularity, when we cross some threshold that moves us into a different world. Earlier this year he gave a series of interviews where he explained, among other things, that

Kurzweil’s most consequential medical date is 2032, when he predicts humanity will reach longevity escape velocity. He defines it as the point at which each passing year brings medical advances that add more than one year to a person’s remaining life expectancy. Chronological time continues, but improvements in prevention, diagnosis and treatment theoretically return more life than aging removes. When Ismail asked for his current date, Kurzweil answered simply: “2032.”

I have watched Kurzweil swallow his dozens of daily pills to make sure he stays alive long enough (he’s arranged to have himself frozen if he dies before Claude can assure his immortality). But even people who haven’t seen this kind of sad spectacle up close have, I think, have some gut reaction that utopia is not billionaires figuring out how to live forever on an overheating planet while entertaining the rest of us with AI “art” that erodes everything that matters about the world. But we have no real way of expressing those fears. Why would Zuckerberg or Sergey Brin or Musk or Bezos listen to us?

Except when we can, in the places where live, manage to block their blasted data centers.

Bill Kristol, the neocon turned never-Trumper, complained the other day that there’s

something bleak about seeing the policy debate over how we ought to shape and regulate this massive, unbelievable, titanic technology collapse down into what’s essentially a NIMBY squabble over where to park the chips that power it.

But that’s wrong, I think. People are rallying where they can, on ground that means something to them. We can’t compete with these guys when it comes to buying elections—Musk alone is pouring $100 million into Senate campaigns in the next few weeks. We can, however, organize in the places we care about, and in the process strike some kind of blow for the things we care about, even if we perceive the threats only dimly. Just as Minnesotans forced the beginnings of a reckoning with our repulsive deportation policies, so people across the country are forcing, as best we can, some kind of conversation about this disfiguring technology. One hopes that it doesn’t bleed over too much into attacks on completely useful technology—in some places the data center fight is leading to solar advocacy, in others to restrictions on solar farms. Resistance is always messy—but right now it’s required.

I remind myself regularly that I grew up in Lexington, Massachusetts, where farmers could not insert themselves into London’s parliamentary debates, and instead used their anger at the high-handedness of colonial authorities to force the start of a conversation on colonialism that’s still underway. We fight where we can and when we can

Share

In other energy and climate news:

+Wanna see a pickup truck going airborne after a Texas heatwave buckles the pavement? Of course you do.

Especially if it comes with a long story about how this is happening all over the place. As Todd Frankel reports,

It was a dramatic example of what has been playing out repeatedly this summer along the nation’s roadways, railroad tracks and bridges: Intense heat is causing surfaces to expand to the point that they break.

The failures illustrate how the nation’s transportation networks, built for a different era, increasingly struggle to handle hotter modern-day summers. And this summer has been brutal. July, federal scientists have said, was the single hottest month on record in the contiguous United States.

Heat waves melt asphalt into goo. Train tracks twist. Overhead power lines sag. Concrete snaps into pieces in what are known as “blowups” — the technical term for what the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation defines as “a heave in a concrete or brick pavement caused by pavement expansion from excessive heat.”

The entire state of Wisconsin was cautioned earlier this summer to “watch for pavement buckles.” A blowup last month closed part of Interstate 97 near Severna Park, Maryland, clogging traffic for a quick repair and then for three straight nights. Interstate 49 in Shreveport, Louisiana, was also shut for hours while crews raced to deal with a blowup. After a bike path next to U.S. 36 buckled, officials in Boulder County, Colorado, warned residents to prepare for more

As long as we’re talking about pickups, the Wall Street Journal had an interesting report on why we can’t have nice things. As Christopher Otts reports, the V-8 engine is back for American pickups, mostly because some buyers can’t deal with the slightly decreased noise level from more efficient engines

What truck buyers and muscle-car fans love more than anything, it turns out, is the rich, throaty roar of a V-8 and the vibrations it causes.

After just one year of its new Hurricane engine, Ram brought back the old eight-cylinder engine to its lineup for 2026 model-year trucks—and it is paying off for parent company Stellantis. Buyers can pick a truck with a Hurricane or pay more for one with an old V-8 engine, called the Hemi. Ram sales are up 22% this year, bucking an industry decline of 3%.

“It just sounds like what a truck should sound like,” said Brian Ewart, a 39-year-old Kansas dad and Navy veteran who recently spent $80,000 on a Ram with the V-8.

+A former Colorado coal mine has been converted to a big solar farm. In fact, the story is even better than that

The Coors coal mine, which lies 40 miles northeast of Denver, operated from 1979 to 1987, then served as a fly ash disposal site until 2016. Since then, the land has sat unused.

Now, Molson Coors' energy is bringing energy production back to the area with a new 47-acre solar panel farm.

That’s right—an abandoned fly ash disposal site is now going to use the sun to brew beer.

+Phoenix firefighters and paramedics have to figure out how to keep people alive in infernal heat. Here’s an excellent short documentary about how they do it. (Lots of ice)

+The summer’s crazy series of European heatwaves is producing, among other things, some very fine journalism. Eric Klinenberg offers up an extended essay on the changing meaning of summer there

“Travelling to European cities is about cultural experience,” Daniel Scott, a scholar of tourism at the University of Waterloo, in Ontario, told me. “Whether it’s Paris, Barcelona, or Rome, you amble around, sightseeing, street shopping, taking a riverboat tour, going to a museum, a restaurant, a café. Most of that time, you’re outside.” Climate change increasingly turns pleasure trips into exercises in escaping pain. “When I’m in Europe, I always notice how many people crowd under trees and shaded areas,” Scott said. “But at some attractions, like the Acropolis, there’s no way to avoid the blazing sun. On especially hot days, they’ve got the Red Cross giving out water, medics pre-positioned because they know many people are going to be in trouble when they come down.”

Meanwhile, the ongoing heat and drought continue to make life difficult for the new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, who would clearly love to prove his centrist moderation by approving some new North Sea oil drilling and gutting EV sales targets, except that people are starting to connect that up with the fact that their country has caught on fire. A bunch of green groups sent him an open letter; meanwhile, here’s the image that Greenpeace managed to make across hundreds of square meters in a scorched field

Of course, you could take the position of UK’s MAGA wing, the Reform party, whose deputy leader last week penned an oped advising overheated Britons to lie back on their recliners and enjoy it.

“When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.”

Right. Just a reminder that there were at least ten thousand “excess deaths” from the heat in June alone across Europe.

+Speaking of “excess deaths,” China has managed to avoid 262,000 of them so far by switching to EVs. As Fred Lambert points out

The study, published May 13 in Nature Health, used high-resolution satellite air-quality data and machine learning to measure pollution across 150 Chinese cities. The researchers compared actual pollution levels to a counterfactual scenario in which every vehicle on the road still ran on an internal combustion engine.

By 2023, the spread of new energy vehicles (NEVs) — a category that includes battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, and hydrogen vehicles — was linked to a 23.80% reduction in fine particulate matter (PM2.5), a drop of 8.97 micrograms per cubic meter. Carbon monoxide fell even further, down 30.67%.

The researchers estimate those air-quality improvements prevented roughly 262,000 non-accidental deaths, along with about 75,000 all-cause deaths.

The numbers matter because outdoor air pollution causes more than 4 million premature deaths worldwide each year, and roughly a quarter of those occur in China.

This is by no means confined to China. A new study shows that children in London have larger and healthier lungs thanks to regulations aimed at reducing car traffic in the city. As Damien Gayle reports

Air pollution from traffic has stunted the development of children’s lungs in London for decades. Previous research found that by the age of eight or nine, children from the most polluted areas had 5-10% less lung capacity than their peers elsewhere.

Meanwhile, China is exporting so many of those lung-saving EVs that they’re running out of ships to carry them on. Paul Berger writes:

Some automakers are so desperate to get vehicles to Europe, Australia and Latin America they are squeezing them inside shipping containers more commonly used to transport furniture, clothes and electronics.

The export supply is now so immense that Chinese automakers are expanding into the shipping sector, too. BYD launched its first dedicated car carrier in 2024 and now has a fleet of eight vessels.

+There’s less English-language reporting about the massive heatwaves that have plagued Asia this year, with country after country setting new records. But this, from Raphael Rashid in Seoul caught my eye

In a potato field in Yanggu county, 80 miles (130km) north-east of Seoul, Lee Sang-hyuk dug into the soil and found nothing worth saving.

A week earlier the crop, located in Gangwon province, had looked fine. Now the potatoes came up soft and collapsing, “like boiled potatoes”, spoiled by heat that had turned the ground into something closer to an oven.

“It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,” he told local broadcaster SBS.

His ruined harvest is one thread in a punishing summer across east Asia, as record heat swept through South Korea, Japan and Hong Kong in recent weeks.

On 2 August, the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5C, the highest registered in South Korea since modern weather observations began in 1904.

The heat has since been blamed for at least 31 deaths nationwide, according to the country’s disease control agency, while more than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have died.

Authorities issued a heat warning, urging people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, told his cabinet the extreme weather was “unlike anything we have experienced before”.

+The first signs of the dawning El Niño are showing up in the Pacific, as David Gelles reports from Kiribati:

Already, around Christmas Island, one of this nation’s 33 atolls and islands, the ocean surface temperature is 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, warmer than usual for this time of year, compared with the previous 30 years. And as much as 10 percent of the corals appeared bleached in a series of dives over the past few days, Atwood said.

“We expect this to get worse and worse and worse until the end of this year,” she said. “This is just the tip of the iceberg.”

+Headed back to college? The good people at Rewild Your Campus are hosting their annual online advocacy bootcamp next month so you can learn how to work with the groundskeepers to make things better. Meanwhile, from Jaimie P. Cloud, a new book for “young people and those who love them” about living well on a working planet

+Sarah Hoffmann reports from inside ALEC (the rightwing legislative lobby) that the fossil fuel industry is counting on a conservative supermarjority in the Supreme Court to protect them from liability for the climate crisis.

“If we had a different Supreme Court, this would be a very different presentation that I’m giving you,” Paul Watkins said during this year’s annual meeting of the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC).

Watkins is the founding partner of Fusion Law, a firm in Arizona that has received millions of dollars from the political network of Leonard Leo, a conservative power broker and co-chairman of the Federalist Society, who is largely credited with orchestrating the Republican takeover of the Supreme Court.

During his late-July presentation to ALEC, a conservative lobbying and advocacy group with a long history of platforming climate denial, Watkins held out hope that the court would deliver a ruling favorable to the oil and gas industry when it considers a major climate lawsuit involving ExxonMobil and the Canada-headquartered company Suncor Energy in October.

“But it’s a good reminder of how close we are to really catastrophic outcomes,” said Watkins, who has played a lead role in Leo-backed campaigns to prevent companies and large financial institutions from considering climate risks in their investment decisions. Watkins, who also served as the inaugural director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Office of Innovation during the first Trump administration, added that a different Supreme Court might allow such a lawsuit to move forward.

Meanwhile, with the redoubtable Sheldon Whitehouse in the lead, 99 Senators and Congressmen filed a friend of the court brief urging the Supremes to let Boulder Colorado have its day in court in the Suncor case.

“In the Clean Air Act, Congress created a comprehensive and detailed system for reducing air pollution,” they wrote. “It did not address deceptive marketing or sales of fossil fuels at all.”

The members of Congress also noted that many of the briefs written in support of Exxon and Suncor were authored by groups or people that have received funding from fossil fuel-linked donors: “These amicus briefs present as an outpouring of support for a legal position, but publicly available information shows them to be funded by a small and powerful phalanx of self-interested entities,” the congressional members write. “These industry front groups and their funders are part of a tightly connected web of organizations dedicated to protecting fossil fuel interests in Congress, at executive agencies, and in the courts.”

+Not only is Zorhan Mamdani bicycling around the city (with a helmet!), he and his team are exploring ways to put the sweltering heat in the city’s subway system to good use with:

a new technology that could cool subway platforms and reuse excess heat to warm nearby city buildings during the winter.

The proposed thermal energy network would be tested at the Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall 4/5/6 and Chambers Street J/Z station complex. Officials said it would be the first project of its kind in a U.S. transit system.

The study comes as the MTA prepares a major overhaul of the aging Chambers Street station. Officials said the location offers a chance to explore ways to address extreme heat, a growing challenge across the subway system.

According to the MTA, Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall is one of the system’s hottest stations, with average summer temperatures reaching 96 degrees Fahrenheit in 2025.

“There are few feelings worse than escaping the extreme summer heat only to find yourself on a subway platform that is even hotter,” Mayor Mamdani said. “We can make our subway platforms cooler and more comfortable while putting wasted heat to work during the winter.”

The proposed system would capture heat from subway platforms, store it underground and redirect it to nearby municipal buildings during colder months. Officials said the project could reduce energy costs while improving conditions for riders.

text:
Employees fund PAC’s direct contributions, but ratepayers are paying twice as much to ‘administer’ fund

Salt River Project (SRP) ratepayers are paying at least $500,000 annually to support the administration of SRP’s political action committee, which works to support and oppose political candidates in Arizona and nationally. The political action committee (PAC) is called SRP’s Political Involvement Committee (PIC). Contributions in support of political campaigns from the PIC are funded by employees’ contributions, typically deducted from their paychecks. But the PIC also has administrative costs, which SRP customers fund through their water bills, according to SRP’s response to questions from the Energy and Policy Institute (EPI). Those ratepayer contributions have exceeded the employee contributions on an annual basis in recent years, according to internal budgets provided by SRP to EPI in response to Arizona public records requests. The PIC’s recent goal is to raise around $566,000 to contribute over a two year election cycle, meaning that customers are paying almost twice as much to administer the PIC as SRP employees are funding in political contributions.

SRP is comprised of two organizations, the Salt River Valley Water Users’ Association, a private water company, and the Salt River Project Agricultural Improvement and Power District, a political subdivision of the State of Arizona, and serves approximately two million power and water customers. SRP formed the PIC in 1976 through the Salt River Valley Water Users’ Association, the private water corporation. SRP’s PIC contributes funds toward candidates for federal, state and local office, as chosen by SRP employees who comprise the PIC Advisory Committee. Employees who contribute to the PIC come from both the power and water sides of SRP. PIC Advisory Committee members are also a mix of employees who work for both sides of the organization.

According to documents obtained by EPI in response to public records requests, SRP’s PIC “is an essential part of SRP and Public Affairs’ engagement strategy.” As of 2023, approximately 19% of SRP’s employees participated in the PIC, “which is 6 points higher than PIC’s peer benchmarking group according to [the] Public Affairs Council’s 2021 PAC Benchmarking Survey.”

SRP has increased the suggested contributions and incentives for employees to contribute in recent years

To fund the PIC, employees choose a contribution amount to deduct from each paycheck. Between 2012 and 2024, the PIC suggested contribution amounts of $20 per pay period for the President’s Club ($520 annual contribution) or $9 per pay period as a Sustaining member ($234 annual contribution). Records obtained by EPI show that at the end of 2023, SRP’s PIC Manager Christina Worden proposed updating the membership and contribution levels, including larger suggestions for employees in leadership or management roles. Worden proposed a suggested contribution schedule as follows:

At the time the PIC proposed increasing employee funding, it was distributing just under $450,000 in a two year election cycle, but had a goal to distribute approximately $566,000 in a cycle. Worden noted in her presentation materials that Arizona’s elections have become more competitive and expensive. She also highlighted the growth in spending by other PACs such as Pinnacle West, parent company of Arizona Public Service, which grew its spending from around $614,000 in 2012 to around $913,000 in 2022.

Worden also proposed incentives to increase participation in the PIC’s new funding levels. These incentives included participation in the ‘76 Club for individuals who are ”early adopters” and recognition at a special event, such as a luncheon with the CEO and President of SRP. Another suggested incentive is to provide a one-time match “with SRP administrative funds” to an individual’s charity of choice, mirroring the person’s contribution to the PIC. EPI asked SRP for comment on the total amount of SRP administrative funds, which are funded by ratepayers, contributed toward the match incentive. SRP stated that in FY 2025, $55,000 of SRP administrative funds were spent toward this match incentive.

SRP PIC administrative costs lack transparency for ratepayers

SRP offers many perks and benefits for employee participants in its PIC. The PIC regularly sponsors lunches, coffee chats, outings to sporting events, picnics, and dinners for employees who contribute to the PIC. Members of the PIC advisory committee, which makes decisions about which candidates receive contributions from the PIC, may also attend a multi-day leadership retreat in Washington, DC. Records obtained by EPI show that in recent years, the PIC sponsored a dozen or more activities for employee contributors annually.

Since 2023, funding for PIC sponsored events has come from SRP’s administrative funds, which are funded by ratepayers. Until fiscal year 2023, SRP did not have a budget for expenses for PIC sponsored events. In fiscal years 2023, 2024, and 2025, SRP allocated $500,000 per year for the PIC’s budget. The budget document provided by SRP in response to EPI’s record requests reports that in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, the entire budget was spent in the category “Professional Development – Memberships/F”. In fiscal year 2025, “Professional Development – Memberships/F” is allocated $2,000 of the budget. The rest of the budget for fiscal year 2025 breaks out into 15 other categories, including “Meals and Entertainment – External Meals,” which is allocated $240,000 of the total budget.

Several of the categories include cut off words, and it is unclear what types of expenses are included in certain categories. The limited detail in the budget and the relatively recent use of a budget at all underscores the lack of transparency around what SRP customers are paying for to support the PIC.

SRP’s PIC contributes in Arizona and across the country

SRP’s PIC contributes to the political campaigns of local, state, and federal candidates in Arizona, as well as state and federal races in other parts of the country. The PIC regularly contributes to Republican and Democratic party offices, candidate affiliated PACs, and PACs for groups such as the Arizona Chamber of Commerce. The contributions are voted on by PIC Advisory Committee members at their monthly meetings.

$7 million awarded to 128 communities since 2023

COLUMBUS, OH (August 21, 2026) - More than $1 million is being invested to help Ohio communities reduce chloride pollution caused by road salt entering waterways, while maintaining public safety on the roads during harsh winter weather.

Ohio EPA is announcing the latest round of H2Ohio chloride reduction grants, awarding $1,078,831 in funding to support 16 projects across the state. H2Ohio is Governor Mike DeWine’s statewide initiative focused on improving Ohio’s water quality. Grants of up to $75,000 will help municipalities purchase equipment or improve salt storage facilities.

“Safe roads and safe water are equally important, and through this program, we can protect both,” said Governor DeWine. “By investing in better salt storage and more efficient equipment, we are reducing unnecessary salt use, protecting water quality, and helping taxpayer dollars go further.”

“These grants are a win for communities, drivers, and Ohio’s waterways,” said Ohio EPA Director John Logue. “Across Ohio, communities continue to invest in the longevity of neighborhoods, and by using this H2Ohio funding and seeing the importance and the difference of using less salt, we collectively are working together to keep our roads and our waterways healthier.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. (Aug. 21, 2026) – The Department of Energy abandoned a project that would bring clean steel production to Ohio by allowing the Cleveland-Cliffs facility in Middletown to instead keep its old, coal-based blast furnace. This decision to upgrade the coal furnace locks in antiquated technology and negative air pollution impacts for the surrounding community.

The stated purpose Congress gave for this program was to finance projects “to accelerate greenhouse gas emissions reduction progress to net-zero.”

The following is a comment from Ian Wells, federal industrial lead advocate at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council):

“Instead of spending these taxpayer funds to ensure cleaner, healthier air for Ohioans, as Congress intended, the Trump administration is running a bait and switch to keep the Cleveland Cliffs blast furnace burning dirty coal for decades to come.

“Clean steel is the future, both for Cleveland-Cliffs and the world, but instead of building a better, healthier future, the Trump administration is trying to tie this facility to technology from a century ago. It’s time to transition away from a reliance on coal, but this administration doesn’t seem to understand that we can create jobs and investments and build a cleaner future if we try. What a shame.”

NRDC is tracking every step of the Trump administration's attacks on public health and the environment. Go to White House Watch for the comprehensive list of these attacks. To subscribe to our weekly newsletter, email jbar@nrdc.org.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contacts: Mark Drajem, mdrajem@nrdc.org

NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council) is an international nonprofit environmental organization with more than 3 million members and online activists. Established in 1970, NRDC uses science, policy, law and people power to confront the climate crisis, protect public health and safeguard nature. NRDC has offices in New York City, Washington, D.C., Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, Beijing and Delhi (an office of NRDC India Pvt. Ltd).

title: The missing $20000 EV: Why small, affordable electric cars don't work on North American roads
description:
Then cross over to China, the world’s largest car market, and cheap electric vehicles are not a niche urban curiosity – they dominate the mainstream sales leaderboards.
In fact, the $10,000 to $20,000 price bracket accounts for nearly half of China’s entire electric vehicle volume.
The cheapest small EV on sale in the North American market today is the Chevrolet Bolt at a starting MSRP of ~$29,900.
Why can’t North American drivers buy a simple, inexpensive electric city car?
The final bits At the end of all this, if you are someone looking for a small $10,000 electric vehicle at your local dealership, chances are that you are going to be disappointed.
text:
In the past 24 hours, the Chinese market saw the debut of three cars priced well under the $20,000 bracket, with those labels being Volkswagen, Hyundai, and MG. These were all sedans. The hatchbacks, on the other hand, cost even less. Let’s skip continents now, shall we? Walk through the historic centers of Paris, Milan, or Amsterdam, and you will quickly realize you are on a “minicar safari”. The tight, centuries-old streets are populated by a diverse ecosystem of electric micro-vehicles.

From the square $6,600 Citroën Ami to the retro Microlino, these tiny battery-powered pods zip through traffic and slip easily into narrow parallel parking spaces that would prove impossible for a standard sedan, let alone a full-sized SUV. We also remember the G-Wiz, which was made in India and sold there and in the UK market. Market reviews called it a “Death Trap,” but it was a popular small electric which made it globally, though it did not make it to North America.

Then cross over to China, the world’s largest car market, and cheap electric vehicles are not a niche urban curiosity – they dominate the mainstream sales leaderboards. Market data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) shows that 70% of battery electric cars sold in China are already cheaper than the average conventional internal combustion car. Budget-friendly entry-level models, such as the Geely Geome Xingyuan (starting around $9,700 USD) and the compact BYD Seagull (starting around $10,000 USD), routinely top monthly sales charts, outperforming expensive luxury options.

In fact, the $10,000 to $20,000 price bracket accounts for nearly half of China’s entire electric vehicle volume. Over the past few years, the likes of Dongfeng, BYD, and Wuling have proved that small cars are the future of mass-market EV adoption. And as such, these cars are now slowly making inroads into the European markets, as well. The US, on the other hand, remains an exception.

Step onto a dealership lot in North America, and these inexpensive, sub-$20,000 commuters are nowhere to be found. The cheapest new electric entry points in the United States and Canada hover around $30,000, while the average new EV transaction price remains well above $30,000. The cheapest small EV on sale in the North American market today is the Chevrolet Bolt at a starting MSRP of ~$29,900. Of course, one could argue the Slate pickup is the cheapest to pre-order right now at $25,000 or $24,950 to be exact, but deliveries are scheduled to go live later this year in North America.

So, we’re back to the Bolt. For comparison, BYD’s Dolphin Mini starts at just over $10,000, packs a LiDAR sensor, and touches 250 miles on a single charge. Why can’t North American drivers buy a simple, inexpensive electric city car? The answer lies in a combination of rigid regulatory classification, a historical culture built on cheap fuel, and an escalating physical safety arms race on American highways.

The regulatory red tape barrier

A primary reason small overseas EVs cannot cross the ocean is the stark difference in how vehicle regulators classify lighter, smaller transport. In Europe, public authorities recognized decades ago that lightweight urban commuters required a distinct regulatory framework. European Union rules created two specific categories for “quadricycles”. These vehicles are speed-capped (typically at 28 mph or 56 mph), limited in weight, and subject to simpler safety standards than full-sized passenger cars. Because quadricycles bypass the multi-million-dollar development costs of full crash-test compliance, manufacturers can sell them at entry-level prices. In many European cities, this category opens up clean mobility to city dwellers, delivery services, and operators as young as 14.

In contrast, the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) maintains a rigid rulebook. As transportation analyst David Zipper points out in Bloomberg CityLab, NHTSA forces four-wheeled vehicles into an unyielding binary: a vehicle must either comply with the exhaustive Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) mandated for full-sized highway automobiles, or it is capped at a maximum speed of 25 mph as a Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV).

NHTSA previously rejected petitions to establish a “medium-speed vehicle” class (which would have covered vehicles traveling up to 35 mph), effectively blocking European quadricycles and cheap Asian city cars from legally operating on normal U.S. streets. To re-engineer an overseas micro-car or sub-$10,000 hatchback to meet North American crash standards, manufacturers would have to add heavy structural steel, advanced bumper assemblies, and complex airbag systems. That engineering overhaul instantly destroys the low-cost appeal, driving the retail price tag closer to $25,000 or $30,000.

Cheap gas and five decades of “car bloat”

Even if regulatory hurdles were removed, micro-cars face an uphill battle against the physical environment of North American roads. As Steve Greenfield of Automotive Ventures notes, a history of low fuel taxes explicitly shaped American infrastructure. Historically, gasoline has been taxed far less in the U.S. than in almost any other developed nation. Cheap fuel allowed generations of drivers to buy progressively larger, heavier, and less fuel-efficient vehicles.

The resulting shift in market distribution over the past 50 years is stark. In 1975, sedans and station wagons made up 80% of all new U.S. vehicle sales, while trucks and SUVs were practically non-existent on consumer driveways. Now, today, sedans and wagons have plummeted to just 25% of new car sales, while trucks and SUVs account for 45% or more of the market.

Because fuel costs were low, town planners and civil engineers built wide multi-lane arterial roads, expansive multi-lane intersections, and oversized suburban parking lots. In an environment designed around wide lanes and high traffic speeds, a 28 mph city pod is not just slow. It struggles to function in daily suburban life.

The highway safety arms race

The prevalence of massive light trucks and heavy passenger vehicles has created a physical arms race that discourages buyers from choosing small cars. When suburban roads are dominated by 6,000-pound gas pickups and 9,000-pound electric SUVs, sitting in a 1,000-pound micro-car feels intimidating.

That fear is rooted in statistical reality. Data cited from The Economist indicates that a driver is seven times more likely to die in a collision when struck by a Ford F-150 compared to a standard Toyota Camry. Independent research from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) confirms that bigger, heavier vehicles consistently afford superior occupant protection during an impact.

As Greenfield observes, as larger vehicles fill suburban neighborhood driveways, the social push to match that vehicle scale increases. Parents shopping for their teenager’s first car actively seek out heavy, high-riding crossovers rather than compact hatchbacks. A sub-$10,000 city car designed for narrow 30 mph urban zones in Europe or Asia simply cannot offer the crash protection demanded by buyers navigating 70 mph North American highways alongside heavy commercial traffic.

The local adaptation

As trade barriers, safety regulations, and road conditions prevent sub-$15,000 overseas city cars from entering local showrooms, automakers are pursuing a different strategy for North America. Rather than importing tiny two-seater pods or bare-bones hatchbacks, domestic and foreign brands are adapting by developing subcompact crossovers like the Kia EV3 and Chevrolet Equinox EV. These models feature smaller footprints and lower price tags relative to full-sized electric trucks, but they retain the higher seating position, extended battery range, and structural crash protection necessary to navigate North American roadways safely.

For budget-conscious drivers who need an affordable commuter today, the takeaway is clear. Waiting for a brand-new $15,000 city EV to land on a local dealership lot is a lost cause. Instead, the real entry point for accessible electric driving has migrated to the pre-owned market. Industry data from Cox Automotive shows that used EV sales surged 10.1% year-over-year in July 2026, reaching nearly 37,000 units sold in a single month.

This rapid growth is being fueled by an influx of off-lease returns and trade-ins, providing secondary market buyers with a vast selection of 3-to-4-year-old models. While newer-generation used models keep the overall category average around $37,800, early-generation high-volume commuters like the Nissan Leaf, Chevrolet Bolt, and Hyundai Kona Electric are routinely changing hands on dealer lots for under $18,000. For everyday commuters, these pre-owned options deliver all the low-running-cost benefits of an electric daily driver without forcing buyers to compromise on North American highway safety.

The final bits

At the end of all this, if you are someone looking for a small $10,000 electric vehicle at your local dealership, chances are that you are going to be disappointed. Between a regulatory system that insists every four-wheeled vehicle be built like an armored tank and an ongoing highway size-war where a Ford F-150 can eat a subcompact for breakfast, tiny European and Asian commuters just do not stand a chance on this side of the pond.

So, unless you plan on navigating your morning interstate commute in a 25 mph Low-Speed Vehicle – praying that the lifted pickup in your rearview mirror spots you before you become a bumper sticker – your best bet for a cheap electric daily driver remains the local used car lot. Think of it as the ultimate North American compromise: letting the car’s first owner take the massive depreciation hit so you can quietly glide past the gas pump for under eighteen grand.

text:
At the 2026 Chengdu Auto Show, SAIC’s MG brand officially launched its new mid-size sedan, the MG 07, and the pricing might genuinely surprise you. According to CarNewsChina, the car is available in seven configurations, with prices ranging from 108,900 yuan to 159,900 yuan, or roughly $16,000 to $23,500, making it one of the most affordable electric cars.

A surprisingly premium design for a $16,000 sedan

The MG 07 stands out with a star-ring light group up front and semi-hidden door handles for a cleaner silhouette. It measures 4,886mm long and rides on a 2,825mm wheelbase, paired with frameless doors, two-tone wheels, and yellow brake calipers. At the back, there’s a through-type taillight and a 5-stage adjustable electric spoiler. You get six paint options, including Morello Purple, Notting Grey, Oxford Blue, Milia Pink, California Blue, and Salt Lake White.

On the powertrain front, MG is offering both EV and PHEV options. The EV runs on an 800V platform, offering up to 315 horsepower and a maximum range of 845km, while the PHEV pairs a 1.5L engine with an electric motor for a combined range that stretches to 1,745km. The 610km range EV trims interestingly use semi-solid batteries from Qingtao, while every other version sticks with CATL‘s more familiar LFP cells.

The cabin is where things get really interesting

The cabin is really well done. You get a wraparound cockpit with a 15.6-inch floating touchscreen running on the 8295P chip. The driver’s seat comes with heating and ventilation, and the passenger side even gets a “Queen” zero-gravity mode. Add in a multi-functional vanity mirror, a 21-speaker sound system, and mCDC active suspension, and the comfort package feels genuinely thought out. MG has also added LiDAR here, powered by Momenta’s R7 world model.

The MG 07’s price might be its biggest selling point

If you already had your eye on the EV version, pre-sales kicked off last month starting at 125,900 yuan, or about $18,600. Deliveries are staggered depending on which range you pick. Go for the 650km version, and you should have it by the end of August. Opt for the longer 845km range instead, and you will need to wait until October.

text:
Overview

The waste and recycling industry’s bid to unwind one of the most consequential PFAS regulations has failed. On August 18, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit denied industry petitions challenging EPA’s 2024 rule designating two forever chemicals, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), as hazardous substances under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA). With the designation intact, the search for liability relief now shifts from the courthouse to Capitol Hill.

The Rule and the Challenge

CERCLA lets EPA designate as hazardous any substance that, when released into the environment, may present substantial danger to the public health or welfare or the environment. See 42 U.S.C.A. § 9602. EPA invoked that authority under Section 102(a), 42 U.S.C. § 9602(a) for the first time in 2024 to reach PFOA and PFOS. As a result, seven trade associations petitioned for review, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the National Waste & Recycling Association (NWRA), the American Chemistry Council, and the Recycled Materials Association. The consolidated case, Chamber of Commerce of the United States v. EPA, No. 24-1193, drew a panel of Judges Millett, Katsas, and Rao, with Judge Millett writing the final decision.

Specifically, petitioners argued: (1) that EPA misread CERCLA’s substantial danger standard; (2) gave inadequate notice of the rule’s cost-benefit analysis; and (3) acted arbitrarily in both the analysis and its decision to regulate amid scientific uncertainty. Ultimately, however, the court rejected each of these arguments in turn.

Why the Court Sided With EPA

On the science, the panel found it unnecessary to fix the precise boundaries of “substantial danger,” since the petitioners did not seriously dispute that PFOA and PFOS can harm human health. EPA’s rule spent three pages cataloging associated health effects, from decreased infant birth weight and cardiovascular impacts to elevated liver enzymes, immunosuppression, and preeclampsia.

On notice, the Administrative Procedure Act asks whether a final rule is a logical outgrowth of the proposal such that affected parties should have anticipated it. The court held that EPA’s final Regulatory Impact Analysis grew logically from the Economic Assessment accompanying the proposed rule. Moreover, the cost data EPA added late merely supplemented the existing record, which does not require an additional comment round.

The court thus distinguished its earlier Owner-Operator decision, where a wholly new methodology drove the rule. Here, EPA employed no novel methodology and merely quantified a prior qualitative analysis at the petitioners’ own urging.

On the economics, the court reviewed EPA’s analysis deferentially, according to a broad zone of reasonable estimation. It determined EPA reasonably explained that marginal cleanup costs would be tempered because treatment infrastructure already exists at many sites, and it reasonably rejected a Chamber-commissioned study built on discussions with industry rather than empirical and decades old data. The court likewise rejected the claim that EPA improperly counted costs as benefits. The agency acknowledged private party costs yet reasonably treated the shift of cleanup expenses from taxpayers to polluters as an advantage aligned with CERCLA’s design. And even amid site-specific uncertainty, the court found EPA had made a reasoned decision to regulate.

The Passive Receiver Argument

The industry’s central concern is liability for “passive receivers”—landfills, recyclers, and water utilities that take in PFAS-laden material but neither made nor profited from the chemicals. That concern flows from CERCLA’s structure: once a substance is designated, the statute imposes liability on four categories of potentially responsible parties (PRPs), from owners and operators to arrangers and transporters. Consequently, liability was found to attach notwithstanding any other provision or rule of law, subject only to narrow defenses for acts of God, war, or an unrelated third party. As applied, that means strict, joint-and-several, and retroactive liability, so one PRP can face the cost of an entire cleanup for waste it did not generate. Designation also triggers duties to report qualifying releases.

The panel was unpersuaded that these consequences fall unfairly on passive receivers. Because CERCLA’s contingent, site specific steps mean liability attaches only after individualized review, the court found the fear that designation leads inevitably to liability misplaced. It stressed that the petitioners have come forward with no evidence that those responsible for the presence of hazardous substances at a site have been unfairly saddled with liability or that the statute’s operation has constrained industry. The court also credited EPA’s reliance on CERCLA’s existing liability limits, including its de minimis, de micromis, and innocent-landowner protections.

Those carveouts, however, are particularly narrow. The municipal solid waste exemption reaches only certain small-volume generators, for example, the de micromis exemption covers only tiny quantities disposed of before April 2001, and the recycling exemption applies to defined scrap materials, not PFAS-bearing waste. None broadly shields landfills or utilities. EPA has tried to fill the gap through its 2024 PFAS Enforcement Discretion and Settlement Policy, in which EPA indicated that it does not intend to pursue passive receivers such as municipal landfills, water utilities, and local fire departments. But that policy is nonbinding, and EPA cannot force private PRPs to waive their contribution rights against passive receivers. EPA itself conceded in September 2025 that the best, most enduring solution to this issue is a statutory fix.

Reaction and the Road Ahead

Reaction to the decision has split predictably. NWRA and the Chamber voiced disappointment and warned of continued uncertainty, while stopping short of committing to an appeal, while observers framed it as confirmation that only Congress can supply what EPA cannot. As a practical matter, the decision changes little. That is because the designation was never suspended during the litigation. As such, entities subject to the designation before the ruling remain subject now.

The more meaningful shift now appears to be strategic. With the rule upheld and administrative relief incomplete, the passive receiver debate returns to a Congress that has stalled on it in the past. Standalone bills, including H.R. 1267 for water and wastewater systems, have failed to advance. The most recent vehicle is a defense-bill amendment: S. Amdt. 6429 to the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), introduced by Senator Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, would shield resource management entities, water and wastewater operators, and others from PFAS liability absent gross negligence or willful misconduct. Whether passive receivers obtain relief now turns on whether that amendment survives the defense authorization process. In the meantime, operators should expect the designation to remain in force.
