General Motors NYSE: GM Chief Financial Officer Paul Jacobson said the automaker’s first half performed “remarkably well,” supporting an increase in full-year guidance, while cautioning that the second half faces pressures from commodity inflation, onshoring costs and vehicle launch activity.

Speaking at a JPMorgan event, Jacobson said consumer demand has remained resilient for GM, including demand for trucks and SUVs as well as performance at GM Financial. He said the company’s results have benefited from inventory and incentive discipline despite widely reported affordability concerns in the auto market.

China JV Extension and EV Capacity Actions

3 Medical Device Stocks Giving Investors a Different Healthcare Play

Jacobson highlighted GM’s agreement to extend its China joint venture with SAIC. He said restructuring actions have made the business more self-funding and capable of delivering more consistent profitability, even if it does not return to the roughly $2 billion in annual earnings GM previously generated in China.

“The effect of the restructuring has made it so that we can self-fund and can be consistent profitability,” Jacobson said. He added that China’s economic challenges have reinforced the value of restructuring the operation when GM did, particularly compared with other foreign automakers operating in the country.

Flying Under the Radar: Lockheed Martin's $2.8B Stealth Setup

The company also reached an agreement with Samsung SDI regarding its Indiana battery plant. Jacobson said the related charge had already been incorporated into GM’s second-half accruals and charges, meaning the agreement did not create a new financial impact. He described the move as part of GM’s effort to reduce EV capacity while maintaining supplier relationships and preserving the ability to expand as EV demand grows.

Jacobson said EV adoption has continued at a slower pace than the industry anticipated several years ago, citing changes in government support. GM was previously configured for annual EV capacity of about 1 million units, while current production is substantially lower, he said.

GM expects 2026 EV losses to improve as lower production reduces variable losses and restructuring actions are completed.

Jacobson described 2027 as a potentially more stable year for EV operations, with volumes possibly increasing from current adoption levels of roughly 5% to 6%.

He said 2028 could bring more significant progress toward profitability as GM introduces LMR battery changes and other vehicle architecture improvements.

Truck Launches, Onshoring and Tariffs

GM is transitioning to a new truck platform that Jacobson said will ramp through 2027 before reaching full capacity. The outgoing trucks, in their final year of production, have continued to perform strongly, he said, without the substantial decline in realized pricing that can typically occur as manufacturers increase incentives on outgoing models.

GM expects new trucks to begin arriving in showrooms in December. The company is also undertaking a new engine-platform rollout and converting its Orion facility from EV to internal-combustion-engine production, including Escalade production. Those changes will create near-term inefficiencies as GM hires and trains workers before output reaches scale, Jacobson said.

He said Orion’s efficiency drag should continue into 2027 but improve as production ramps, particularly toward the second half of that year. GM expects increased domestic output to reduce some tariff exposure as it moves toward 2 million units of production through 2027 and into 2028, although Jacobson said it was too early to provide formal tariff guidance because of uncertainty around future trade rates and agreements.

On commodities, Jacobson said GM could see more stable conditions next year if current conditions normalize, but added that geopolitical developments and tariff policies involving Mexico and Canada could materially change the outlook.

Warranty, Supply Chain and Capital Allocation

Jacobson said GM expects a year-over-year warranty improvement of approximately $1 billion to $1.5 billion, but stressed that the company still has substantial work to do. He said warranty costs have risen because of dealership inflation and significant supplier-related issues, including the L87 matter referenced during the discussion.

GM has redirected some inventory and parts to customer-care operations, a decision Jacobson said has at times affected production but helps return customer vehicles to service more quickly. Improving quality and reducing warranty liabilities remain priorities, he said.

The company also announced a $4.5 billion purchasing facility led by JPMorgan and Santander. Jacobson said the facility will help GM build strategic inventory worldwide to protect production and cash flow against supply shortages, geopolitical disruptions and natural disasters. He said the facility will add some interest expense but was structured to support supply-chain continuity.

Regarding EV restructuring cash costs, Jacobson said GM spent about $4.5 billion in the first half and expects most of the remaining spending to occur this year, with some potentially extending into 2027. He said GM has sought to move quickly with suppliers, even if that meant paying more in some cases, to allow the supply base to focus on future product development.

Software, Defense and International Operations

Jacobson said GM’s China software platform has been rated more highly than many Chinese competitors’ platforms, though it cannot simply be transferred to the U.S. market. Still, he said the experience has increased GM’s confidence in its technology capabilities and in the potential for digital revenue growth.

He said about 30% to 40% of Super Cruise customers renew their subscriptions after the initial three-year period. GM plans to make Super Cruise standard on higher-trim Silverado and Sierra trucks, aiming to increase installed volume and build future digital revenue opportunities. Jacobson also pointed to a planned technology shift for Super Cruise with the next-generation Escalade IQ in 2028.

In international markets, Jacobson said Chinese competition is a significant challenge, though GM has continued to benefit from customer and brand loyalty in regions including South America and the Middle East. Disruptions in the Middle East have pressured GM International, but GM has redirected some vehicles to North America at slightly higher margins, he said.

Jacobson also said GM’s defense business has expanded its revenue base and reached break-even, aided by the Infantry Squad Vehicle program. He said the company sees defense as a future margin contributor through opportunities that apply GM engineering and manufacturing capabilities with relatively low capital requirements.

About General Motors (NYSE:GM)

General Motors Company NYSE: GM is a global automotive manufacturer headquartered in Detroit, Michigan, that designs, builds and sells cars, trucks, crossovers and electric vehicles, and provides related parts and services. Founded in 1908, GM has long been one of the world's largest automakers and has evolved into a multi-brand company whose primary marques include Chevrolet, GMC, Cadillac and Buick. Beyond vehicle manufacturing, GM's operations encompass vehicle financing, connected services and advanced mobility initiatives.

GM develops and markets a broad portfolio of products and technologies, including internal-combustion and battery-electric vehicles, vehicle components and on-board connectivity services.

Customers can access tools to track energy use and find assistance resources

CHARLOTTE, N.C. , Aug. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As high temperatures continue across much of North Carolina and South Carolina, Duke Energy is reminding customers about tools that can help them stay informed about their energy use and connect them with assistance programs if they need help.

The reminder comes as federal climate data shows July 2026 was the hottest month ever recorded across the contiguous United States, according to NOAA.

"Summer weather can have a significant impact on how much energy a household uses," said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy'sNorth Carolina president. "We're helping customers stay informed with tools that explain how weather and other factors can affect energy use, while also connecting customers with assistance resources when they need support."

Tools that help customers stay informed

Duke Energy offers several tools that can help customers monitor and better understand their energy use.

Bill Insights in the Duke Energy app helps explain factors that may be affecting energy use and monthly bills, including weather and other changes that can influence energy use.

Usage Alerts help customers track energy use during their billing cycle and provide projected energy use and estimated bill information before the bill arrives. This gives customers time to make adjustments to help reduce energy use before the bill arrives.

Home Energy Reports compare a home's energy use with similar homes and offer tips that can help customers better understand energy use at home.

Help is available

Customers who need help paying their bill are encouraged to contact Duke Energy to learn about payment arrangements and assistance programs.

Resources include:

Payment Assistance Finder , an online tool that helps customers find local agencies and nonprofit organizations that may be able to help. Through partnerships with community organizations across North Carolina, programs such as Share the Light Fund® and Share the Warmth have distributed more than $31 million over the past decade to support customers facing financial hardship.

Share the Light Fund ® , which provides bill-payment assistance for eligible customers experiencing financial hardship.

Payment arrangements and installment plans for eligible customers who need additional flexibility.

Customers can learn more about tools, assistance programs and other resources on Duke Energy'sSummer Energy Solutions webpage.

Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.

Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.

title: The ASEAN Power Grid꞉ Why every year of delay matters - Ember Energy
description:
The ASEAN Power Grid (APG) has been discussed for decades yet built only in fragments.
For instance, land-constrained Singapore could meet part of its growing electricity demand by importing solar power from Cambodia, wind power from Viet Nam and hydropower from Sarawak.
Global technology companies like Microsoft, Google and Amazon increasingly sign long-term renewable energy procurement agreements due to corporate commitment to renewable energy.
Existing and planned interconnector capacities were taken from the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) ASEAN Power Grid Interconnection Profiles.
The model framework is based on TZ-OSeMOSYS that minimises the total discounted cost of the regional power system over the planning horizon.
text:
The ASEAN Power Grid (APG) has been discussed for decades yet built only in fragments. Our modelling shows that one year of slippage beyond the commercial operation date of 2035 will add $2.6 billion in economic losses, accumulating to over $14 billion in five years. Delays will also fundamentally alter the region’s energy transition path as countries get locked in imported fossil fuels for capacity that will still be running in the 2050s. Execution, rather than agreement or capital, is now the constraint for the APG.

ASEAN aims to become the world’s fourth-largest economy by 2045, and electricity sits at the centre of that ambition. Demand is climbing with rising cooling needs, industrial growth, data centres and electrification, yet fossil fuels still meet most of it: coal and gas generated over 73% of the region’s electricity demand in 2025, against around 5% from solar and wind combined.

The region is increasingly reliant on fossil fuels it does not produce, and two energy crises since 2020 have shown the risks of such import dependency. The Middle East supplies about a third of ASEAN’s oil and refined products, and renewed conflict there pushed regional gas prices up by as much as 60% against pre-conflict levels, feeding directly into household bills. Subsidies absorb part of the shock but cannot eliminate the underlying vulnerability. For economies that depend on affordable power to support industry and attract investment, this exposure is a major risk to economic competitiveness.

The APG offers a solution by linking national power systems. It harnesses the pooling effect of geographic diversity, balancing the variability of solar and wind generation, enabling the sharing of reserve capacity, optimising renewable resources across the region and enhancing system security, reliability and market efficiency. The Lao PDR–Thailand–Malaysia–Singapore Power Integration Project (LTMS-PIP) already shows that cross-border interconnections work even across very different market designs, connecting a liberalised market to state-owned utilities through sustained coordination rather than structural harmonisation.

1.2 A connected region can achieve far more than isolated countries

The APG is a critical infrastructure to empower regional economic integration, strengthening energy security and accelerating the region’s energy transition. By connecting national power systems, it smooths the variability of solar and wind generation, enables the sharing of reserve capacity, optimises renewable resources across the region and enhances system security, reliability, and market efficiency.

Interconnection enables greater renewable energy integration by harnessing the pooling effect of geographic diversity in both renewable generation and demand profile. Connecting dispersed renewable resources allows surplus generation in one area to offset local shortages caused by diurnal cycles or seasonal variations elsewhere, reducing the need for conventional plants or battery storage to balance variability. Modelling suggests that robust cross-border interconnection can reduce storage requirements in ASEAN by up to 50%, avoiding substantial upfront investment in battery capacity.

The APG also leverages diversity in load profile. Peak demand occurs at different times across Southeast Asia due to differences in time zones, weather, economic activity and consumption patterns. For example, in 2024, Malaysia’s daily peak demand coincided with that of neighbouring Thailand or Singapore on only around 30% of days. By pooling these diverse demand profiles, the region no longer needs to maintain enough capacity to meet the sum of every country’s individual peak demand simultaneously. Instead, countries can share generation and reserves, reducing the need for standby peaking capacity, lowering system costs and improving overall asset utilisation. An ASEAN study found that while cross-border transmission accounts for less than 0.5% of total system costs, it reduces cumulative system costs by up to 11.9%.

In addition, the APG enables renewable energy to be developed where resources are most abundant and cost-effective, which reduces land requirements and improves resource utilisation. For instance, land-constrained Singapore could meet part of its growing electricity demand by importing solar power from Cambodia, wind power from Viet Nam and hydropower from Sarawak. At the same time, the APG creates significant economic opportunities for resource-rich countries such as Indonesia and Lao PDR by allowing them to monetise their renewable resources through electricity exports. The ASEAN Centre of Energy estimates that more than 60 GW of solar and wind capacity has been identified along APG corridors, representing a substantial pipeline of projects to support the region’s energy transition.

Beyond enhancing operational flexibility, regional interconnection strengthens energy security by enabling greater renewable energy integration, therefore reducing reliance on gas imports and the associated geopolitical risks such as the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

Interconnection also provides critical contingency support, enhancing reliability during emergency events, which is especially valuable for regions prone to extreme weather events such as typhoons and floods, such as ASEAN, where unplanned outages are more frequent. The World Bank estimates the economic costs for power outages during two dry months in Viet Nam in 2023 are about $1.4 billion.

2.1 Base case: the APG will enable rapid renewable build-out and cross-border electricity trade

While the ASEAN Ministers on Energy Meeting (AMEM) targets the full realisation of the APG by 2045, this analysis assumes that all transmission projects associated with Singapore and other priority projects will achieve commercial operation dates (CODs) by 2035, aligned with Singapore’s target to import 6 GW of low-carbon electricity by 2035. The only exceptions are the interconnection projects linking Lao PDR with Cambodia and Myanmar, which are assumed to be commissioned by 2030 based on projections from the ASEAN Centre for Energy.

While some projects, such as the Peninsular Malaysia–Singapore Interconnection, have announced target CODs as early as 2030, a 2035 timeline is considered more realistic given the long development lead times associated with subsea cable projects and cross-border transmission infrastructure in general.

Clean power dominates the regional mix under least-cost optimisation

In the base case, meeting the projected electricity demand across the region requires approximately 400 GW of additional generation and storage capacity by 2040. Clean energy emerges as the optimal expansion pathway, accounting for more than 90% of total capacity additions over the planning horizon.

Benefiting from the location within the sunbelt region, with abundant year-round solar resources and rapidly declining capital costs, solar PV represents the largest share of new capacity, contributing over 250 GW by 2040 in ASEAN. Additionally, the modelling projects ASEAN to develop more than 26 GW of wind capacity, 34 GW of hydropower and up to 46 GW of battery storage over the next 15 years to support system flexibility and renewable integration.

In the cost-optimal pathway, a reduction of over 3 GW of coal is also projected by 2040, primarily due to plant retirement without any new-built replacement. In many countries in ASEAN such as Malaysia and Thailand, there have been announcements that coal will not be considered for expansion, whereas countries like Viet Nam plan to peak coal capacity in 2030 and phase out thereafter.

2.2 Delay scenario and sensitivity case: the cost of delaying the APG

An interconnected ASEAN by 2035 will unlock a highly efficient renewable energy system, with cross-border trade exceeding 120 TWh annually. Our modelling shows that the delay of construction will leave ASEAN behind not only with fossil lock-in but also with a huge amount of costs.

This section evaluates the effects of project delays by comparing the delay scenario with the base case, which assumes most of APG will be commissioned by 2035. In the delay scenario, all interconnection projects scheduled for commissioning in the base case are assumed to be deferred by one year.

Although the postponement is relatively short with only one year, the results reveal substantial regional consequences by 2040, including economic losses of $2.6 billion, increased gas consumption by over 12 billion cubic metres, and 42 million tonnes of higher CO2 emissions. These findings underscore the importance of delivering transmission infrastructure on schedule to fully realise the benefits of regional power integration.

Cost of delay accumulates: One year $2.6 billion accumulates to $14 billion over five years

Since delaying the interconnections alters the model’s objective function over the entire planning horizon to 2040, the optimisation problem of the delay scenario differs from that of the base case. Consequently, the impacts are assessed using cumulative outcomes through 2040 rather than considering 2035 alone.

Across the region, the delay scenario incurs substantially higher fuel costs due to reduced renewable capacity additions resulting from the absence of the APG by 2035. Cumulative fuel expenditures of the delay scenario by 2040 are about $5.6 billion greater than in the base case.

In contrast, the interconnections enable greater deployment of capital-intensive renewable generation by 2035 in the base case compared to the delay scenario. As a result, cumulative capital expenditures by 2040 in the base case (about $424 billion) exceed those in the delay scenario (about $421 billion) by more than $3 billion. Nevertheless, the savings in fuel costs outweigh these additional investments. Overall, commissioning the APG in 2035 rather than 2036 yields a net regional benefit of approximately $2.6 billion.

A one-year delay in the APG also increases cumulative gas consumption by about 12 bcm, which is higher than Singapore’s gas consumption in 2024 at 11 bcm. If this gas volume was sourced from imports, the amount is equivalent to the cargo capacity of roughly 78 Q-Max LNG carriers. The Q-Max vessel is currently the largest LNG carrier in the world, each capable of transporting around 260,000 m³ of LNG, assuming that the volume reduction ratio from gas to LNG is 600 times.

Environmentally, the delay scenario results in an addition of more than 42 mtCO2 emissions. Offsetting this amount would require approximately 46 million trees growing for 50 years, assuming an average sequestration rate of 18.3 kg CO2 per tree per year.

A longer delay of the APG by five years could impose an additional cost of approximately $14 billion on ASEAN by 2040. These higher costs would ultimately be borne by consumers, either directly through higher electricity prices or indirectly through government subsidies.

Additionally, the five-year delay increases cumulative gas consumption by more than 55 bcm by 2040, a volume which exceeds 2024 gas consumption of Thailand at 42 bcm and Singapore at 11 bcm combined, and raises CO2 emissions by over 71 million tonnes – an amount almost equivalent to the Philippines’ power sector emissions in 2025.

On a national level, without the APG to supply the rising demand, Singapore must install an additional 300 MW of gas-fired capacity to meet demand in 2035. Although renewable imports enabled by the interconnections eliminate the need for this capacity from 2036 onwards, gas plants typically have economic lifetimes of around 25 years and a minimum take-or-pay contract of about 70%, thereby increasing long-term fuel costs due to the lock-in of gas-fired infrastructure.

In the delay scenario, as the APG is completed in 2036, greater renewable energy deployment occurs after that point. However, because additional battery storage and gas capacity had already been built to meet demand in 2035, these long-lived assets remain in the system, limiting further renewable capacity expansion by 2040. As a result, compared with the base case, the delay scenario retains around 200 MW more battery storage and 400 MW more gas capacity, but develops 1.4 GW less hydropower by 2040.

A one-year delay of the regional interconnection will increase gas generation by over 50 TWh

As a consequence of the reduced renewable build-out, to fill in the missing supply of renewables, gas-fired generation increases by more than 50 TWh across the region by 2040, roughly 3.6% of ASEAN electricity demand in 2025. Our modelling reflects that one of the most important roles of the APG is moving cheap renewable energy from where it is to demand centres that are overwhelmingly gas-fired, such as Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia. Without the interconnection, those systems simply serve that demand with their own gas-fired power plants.

Besides that, a one-year delay to the APG would dismiss the supply of more than 36 TWh of renewable electricity, including over 13 TWh of solar. Export-oriented renewable projects in Sumatra, Cambodia, Lao PDR and Myanmar depend on transmission links to secure long-term off-take agreements and financing. Without the interconnectors, these projects are unlikely to proceed. The consequences extend well beyond the one-year delay, as investment decisions deferred during that period are replaced by gas-fired plants, for example the 300 MW in Singapore, which typically remain in operation for 20–30 years. The result is not a temporary supply shortfall, but a long-term fossil fuel lock-in.

This analysis assumes that cross-border trade is driven by least-cost optimisation under the projected price trajectory. In practice, whether interconnection displaces gas or simply enables continued gas trading between systems depends on relative nodal price signals such as locational marginal pricing and on governance mechanisms such as carbon tax and emission accounting framework. These instruments will be discussed further in Section 3.2 and are essential to ensure interconnectors are primarily used to move clean generation rather than fossil-fired power.

3.1 Challenges

The modelling in Chapter 2 highlighted the significant economic loss of delaying the APG. It is now important to assess the reasons behind the bottleneck of implementation. This subchapter lists the issues that cause the delay of APG projects.

Authority gap, regulatory constraint and implementation challenges

One of the APG’s biggest hurdles is the institutional gap. Fragmented regulatory frameworks with the absence of harmonised technical and market rules continue to slow down progress. Multiple ASEAN bodies coordinate planning, yet none possess the authority to enforce decisions, drive project implementation or mandate the real-time cross-border data sharing needed for efficient power trading.

However, global experience demonstrates that cross-border market integration does not need to wait for fully developed institutions. For example, the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E), which holds regional institutions to issue legally binding obligations to national system operators, was established in 2008, two years after the first multilateral market coupling in Europe in 2006. Given ASEAN’s decentralised governance model, ASEAN members will need innovative institutional arrangements that strengthen regional coordination while respecting national sovereignty.

National regulations also create barriers to investment and cross-border electricity trade. In Indonesia, for example, third-party access to electricity transmission infrastructure is not permitted, limiting opportunities for private sector participation in regional interconnection projects. Indonesia also requires renewable electricity export permits to be renewed every five years, whereas investors typically require 20–25 years of regulatory certainty to finance capital-intensive infrastructure such as renewable power plants or subsea interconnectors. This mismatch between regulatory timeframes and investment horizons substantially increases project risk and financing costs.

Beyond governance and regulation, cross-border transmission projects face complex permitting and implementation challenges. Transmission corridors frequently traverse environmentally sensitive or protected areas, requiring extensive environmental assessments and stakeholder consultation. Land acquisition, social opposition and the technical complexity of constructing long-distance transmission infrastructure can further delay project development and increase costs.

Financial, market and technical hurdles

Bankability is another major block for progress with the APG. The International Energy Agency estimates that APG interconnections require around $27 billion by 2040. This can rise to $100 billion by 2045 if domestic grid upgrades are included, according to the Asian Development Bank. Even though quite substantial, the required investments are likely to be manageable if capital from multilateral banks and private investors is effectively mobilised. Yet clean power capital continues to be underestimated. ASEAN invests only $0.80 in clean energy for every $1 spent in fossil fuels, which is far behind the global average of $2 to $1. To shift capital allocation, the region urgently needs investment-ready interconnection projects.

The main barriers to bankability are back to regulatory and market constraints such as lengthy permitting processes, regulatory uncertainty and inconsistent market frameworks across ASEAN.

Transmission projects often require approvals from multiple agencies and jurisdictions, extending development timelines and increasing financing costs. Investors also face uncertainty over licensing arrangements, wheeling charges, transmission tariffs and cost recovery mechanisms. Such prolonged regulatory processes weaken project economics by delaying revenues and increasing development risk, making it more difficult to secure long-term financing.

Cross-border subsea transmission projects face additional technical and commercial challenges. High-voltage direct current (HVDC) submarine cables require significant upfront capital investment and typically have development timelines of 10–12 years. Routing must avoid submarine volcanoes, seismic zones, deep ocean trenches and busy shipping and fishing corridors, while projects might face environmental side effects, social protest and difficulty of construction. Global supply chain constraints can further complicate deployment. Prices for power transformers and submarine cables have nearly doubled since 2018, manufacturing capacity remains constrained and specialised cable-laying vessels are operating close to full utilisation worldwide, with only a handful capable of installing the HVDC subsea cables.

Financing conditions in ASEAN also remain less favourable than in advanced economies. Higher financing costs, exchange rate risks and the limited borrowing capacity of many state-owned utilities reduce the attractiveness of large transmission investments. Uncertainty over who should finance, own and recover the costs of cross-border transmission assets further complicates investment decisions.

Differences in electricity market structures also present a major obstacle to regional integration. ASEAN comprises a mix of vertically integrated state-owned electricity systems and liberalised wholesale markets, such as those in Singapore and the Philippines. These incompatible market architectures create challenges for dispatch, settlement, pricing and congestion management in cross-border electricity trading. Developing mechanisms that allow these different market models to operate together will require close government cooperation and harmonised regional market rules.

Finally, investment risks extend beyond construction and financing. Developers face uncertainty over the allocation of commercial risks between governments, utilities and private investors. Reliance on retail off-take models can expose projects to counterparty risk, as demonstrated during Singapore’s 2022 energy crisis when several electricity retailers exited the market. Establishing robust long-term contractual frameworks and clear risk-sharing arrangements will therefore be essential to attract private investment into regional transmission infrastructure.

3.2 Recommendations

The challenges are solvable, but overcoming them requires a shift in political focus, from setting ambitions to sustained implementation. This means continuing to strengthen long-term political commitment, improve regional collaboration to make projects bankable and standardise bilateral arrangements while building the foundations for more sophisticated multilateral trading. This subsection lists the ways to make those changes and help address the barriers delaying the APG.

Political discourse needs to shift from keen discussion to sustained commitment and active coordination

Despite the strong technical and economic case for regional electricity trade, integration ultimately depends on political trust, sustained leadership and effective cooperation. Although cross-border interconnections can reduce system costs and improve energy security, they also require significant upfront investment and create deeper regional interdependence, raising concerns around sovereignty, reliability and equitable benefit sharing. Since transmission infrastructure requires decade-long development timelines, sustained political commitment that spans beyond political cycles is essential to translate regional ambitions into lasting, long-term cooperation.

The Lao PDR–Thailand–Malaysia–Singapore Power Integration Project (LTMS-PIP) proves it is doable. This case demonstrates that connecting different market designs, such as Singapore’s liberalised system and neighbouring state-owned utilities, does not require total structural harmonisation. Instead, it requires active coordination. The LTMS-PIP took more than one hundred working groups, alongside a shared digital coordination platform, to facilitate system balancing and operational alignment. Effective information sharing and institutionalised cooperation mechanisms are therefore key to scaling regional electricity trade in ASEAN.

Address financial risks and uncertainty to unlock investments

The bankability of cross-border transmission infrastructure in ASEAN is shaped by revenue frameworks, financing conditions and the broader policy environment. Unlike domestic generation assets, regional transmission projects depend on complex arrangements for cost recovery across multiple jurisdictions, making revenue certainty and tariff design central to investment viability.

A key gap is the absence of harmonised and transparent transmission tariff frameworks. Tariff structures directly affect project economics and the final electricity price for end-users, yet current arrangements are largely negotiated on a case-by-case basis with no standardised approach to allocating costs, risks and benefits across countries. As a result, transaction structures are complex, slow to negotiate and difficult to scale. Regionally coordinated wheeling charges and transmission tariffs that ensure cost recovery, economic efficiency, fairness, transparency and predictability would improve price visibility, reduce transaction costs and strengthen investor confidence.

Commercial arrangements should also progressively shift from bespoke contracts toward more regulation-based frameworks. Regional models such as the West African Power Pool, which introduced coordinated approaches to transmission charging, demonstrate how greater standardisation can improve investment visibility and reduce transaction costs. Ideally, cost sharing should be done according to a beneficiary pays principle, where the costs are shared in proportion to each party’s received benefits.

In addition, international experience has highlighted the value of leveraging dedicated regional financing mechanisms. For example, the Connecting Europe Facility for Energy provides public funding for energy projects that benefit multiple countries, which recognises that cross-border projects can deliver benefits beyond the country where the infrastructure is built. In ASEAN, initiatives such as the ASEAN Power Grid Financing Initiative (APGFI) can play an important role in mobilising capital by using support from multilateral development banks and private investors to de-risk early-stage APG projects, funding feasibility studies, standardising financing approaches and further crowding in private capital.

Additional revenue stabilisation mechanisms could also enhance bankability. Availability-based payment structures, as used in Brazil, provide predictable long-term income streams that reduce revenue volatility and improve financing conditions for capital-intensive grid infrastructure.

Another way to unlock green finance in cross-border interconnection investment is to build a regional framework for carbon accounting. Harmonised methodologies such as Energy Attribute Certificates (EACs) for measuring the carbon intensity of imported electricity can allow end-users to substantiate and report progress on emissions avoided through grid connections. Additionally, to provide stronger and more consistent price signals for low-carbon electricity, it is important to continue strengthening the scale-up of market-based carbon instruments, such as carbon tax or emission trading schemes. This is particularly relevant for markets such as Singapore, where carbon pricing plays an important role in shaping electricity import economics.

Finally, emerging corporate demand for clean electricity presents a significant opportunity to strengthen project bankability. Global technology companies like Microsoft, Google and Amazon increasingly sign long-term renewable energy procurement agreements due to corporate commitment to renewable energy. Initiating and streamlining supportive policies such as Cross-border Power Purchase Agreement and 24/7 Carbon-Free Energy framework can attract corporate capital, which provides stable, long-term revenue streams that help anchor financing for large-scale cross-border renewable energy and transmission infrastructure in ASEAN.

Start with bilateral projects but switch to multilateral power trade in the long run

Although LTMS-PIP is often described as ASEAN’s first multilateral power trade initiative, in practice it remains a series of coordinated bilateral contracts rather than a fully integrated regional electricity market. While this structure has been effective for initial cross-border projects, it does not yet fully unlock the benefits of multilateral power trade (MPT), particularly in terms of optimising interconnector utilisation and enabling broader system-wide efficiency. MPT arrangements can enhance bankability by increasing utilisation of cross-border interconnectors from around 60% under bilateral trading arrangements to as high as 90%. While bilateral arrangements remain more pragmatic in the near term due to lower requirements for institutional harmonisation and faster implementation timelines, the governance and institutional frameworks for the APG should be built for easy expansion to MPT in the future.

A mature MPT framework would allow interconnectors to be used more efficiently by enabling power flows based on system-wide optimisation rather than bilateral arrangements alone. By expanding the geographic and technological diversity of supply, MPT would improve system flexibility, reduce costs and enhance renewable energy utilisation.

A key principle guiding ASEAN discussions is that MPT development should proceed on a layered market approach and voluntary and stepwise basis. This allows the coexistence of multiple trading mechanisms without a central authority imposing a unified market design. Such an authority, however, will be required for the future fully integrated regional market. Multilateral cross-border markets are expected to evolve gradually through coordination supported by regional institutions and development partners, broadly similar to approaches observed in other federated electricity markets, such as those in Africa and Central America.

In this context, a subregional-led pathway is suitable to advance MPT by building on existing bilateral initiatives such as LTMS and the BIMP interconnections, alongside the introduction of secondary short-term energy trading mechanisms among already interconnected countries. These would allow generation surpluses and deficits to be traded on a voluntary basis, with the system gradually expanding in geographic scope and market sophistication over time towards a fully integrated regional platform.

Ongoing initiatives such as the ASEAN Interconnection Masterplan Study III (AIMS III) Phase 3, including guidelines on regional planning, minimum technical standards harmonisation and implementation strategy, represent important steps toward progressively enabling a more integrated multilateral power trade framework in ASEAN.

Cross-border interconnection and identified renewable energy resources along the corridors

The ASEAN Power Grid (APG) shown in the infographic in Section 1.2 covers the entire region, while the modelling in Chapter 2 covers only part of the network, as described in the “Scope and modelling framework” section below. The infographic includes only existing grid-to-grid interconnections. Existing and planned interconnector capacities were taken from the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) ASEAN Power Grid Interconnection Profiles. For planned projects, the higher capacity from the updates provided by HAPUA Working Group 2 and the AIMS III Phase 1 and Phase 2 ASEAN Renewable Energy Target Scenario was used. The Singapore–Sarawak interconnector was additionally included based on the Energy Market Authority (EMA)’s 2025 announcement.

Solar and wind energy resources along the interconnector corridors were identified primarily using the ACE report above. Cambodia’s renewable resources were based on EMA’s announcement on electricity imports from Cambodia, while hydropower resources in Sarawak were based on EMA’s announcement on electricity imports from Sarawak. Lao PDR’s onshore wind and hydropower resources were based on announcements from the Lao government and project developers. Myanmar’s hydropower resources were based on the country’s Energy Master Plan. Finally, Viet Nam’s offshore wind resources were based on EMA’s announcement on electricity imports from Viet Nam.

Scope and modelling framework

The study examines the potential impacts of delaying ASEAN cross-border electricity interconnectors during the planning horizon from 2025 to 2040. The geographical scope includes Viet Nam, Lao PDR, Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar, Singapore, Peninsular Malaysia and Indonesia’s Sumatra, as these areas exhibit the highest demand for cross-border electricity trading and have the most active interconnection initiatives based on recent government announcements. Other APG projects are excluded from this study and will be considered in future work.

As a result, the modelling outputs presented in Chapter 2 are limited to this geographical scope. For brevity, however, the general terms ASEAN, regional interconnections and APG are used throughout the chapter but only refer to this particular scope of the region.

A quantitative modelling approach was employed using TransitionZero’s Scenario Builder platform to model long-term capacity expansion. The model framework is based on TZ-OSeMOSYS that minimises the total discounted cost of the regional power system over the planning horizon. The model optimises the location, technology and capacity of electricity generation while simultaneously determining electricity flows across the transmission network, considering localised generation costs, resource availability and transmission capacities.

Data and assumptions

Electricity demand projections were compiled from the latest national planning documents where available. Demand for Myanmar and Lao PDR is based on the WWF report Towards a Green and Inclusive Power Sector in the Greater Mekong Subregion. Thailand’s demand follows the Draft Power Development Plan (PDP) 2024, with demand from 2038 to 2040 projected using the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over 2025-2037. Viet Nam follows the Revised Power Development Plan VIII (RPDP 8, 2025). Cambodia adopts Scenario 2 from the Draft PDP 2024. Demand for Peninsular Malaysia is derived from the Report on Peninsular Malaysia Generation Development Plan 2020 (2021–2039), with annual electricity demand extrapolated from projected peak demand. Singapore uses the upper-bound electricity demand forecast published by the Energy Market Authority (EMA), accounting for the projected growth of data centres’ demand with the assumption that the annual growth rate during 2035–2040 remains equal to that observed between 2033 and 2034. Electricity demand for Indonesia’s Sumatra is based on Indonesia’s RUPTL 2025, with demand beyond 2035 projected using the CAGR over the period 2025–2034.

Only existing grid-to-grid transmission projects are considered in this study. All planned interconnectors are assumed bidirectional to evaluate the potential of multilateral power trading, except for the two lines from Indonesia’s Sumatra and Peninsular Malaysia to Singapore being unidirectional due to the vast imbalance of import needs between the regions.

Generation capital costs (CAPEX) are sourced from multiple references. Viet Nam adopts technology cost assumptions from the Danish Energy Agency’s (DEA) Viet Nam Technology Catalogue. Indonesia’s Sumatra uses the DEA Indonesia Technology Catalogue. Coal, gas, solar and wind technologies for Thailand and Malaysia are based on BloombergNEF reports specific to each country. Cambodia, Lao PDR and Myanmar are assumed to have CAPEX values equal to the average of Viet Nam and Thailand, while Singapore adopts the higher CAPEX values between Malaysia and Indonesia to reflect its relatively higher development costs.

Fuel price assumptions for coal and gas are based on the International Energy Agency’s World Energy Outlook 2025 under the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS). Prices are calculated as the average of the European Union, Japan and China values. Milestone year fuel prices for 2035 and 2050 are interpolated exponentially over the remaining modelling years. Biomass fuel cost is assumed to be $32 per tonne in 2024 based on an ERIA report, with an energy content of 17 GJ per tonne and an annual cost escalation of 5%.

All other techno-economic parameters follow the default dataset provided in Scenario Builder documentation. Raw outputs of base case and delay scenarios can be downloaded from the platform.

Limitations

Due to computational constraints, the model contains several limitations. These include an annual 32-time-slice temporal resolution and the exclusion of transmission losses, which can potentially lead to an overestimation of the benefits of long-distance electricity trade. In addition, the analysis is limited to capacity expansion optimisation and does not include chronological economic dispatch modelling. Finally, transmission cost overrun due to delays is also not considered in this study even though it often occurs in practice and could significantly increase the costs of delaying.

text:
Plug-in solar, also known as “balcony solar” is a new category of small, portable solar system that plugs directly into a wall outlet.

The concept took off in Germany in the 2010s with more than one million plug-in solar devices now registered. With ten U.S. states having adopted plug-in solar legislation with more to come, it’s beginning to take off in the U.S. as well. State legislation has many commonalities including interconnection exemption, wattage limits and safety certification.

While plug-in solar can still be used in states that have not passed legislation, potential users may have to apply to the local utility for interconnection approval. Most state legislation exempts the small systems from required interconnection agreements and approvals, which eliminates permitting and interconnection delays and associated fees.

Most state legislation has other similarities, for example, a wattage limit. Most have set a wattage limit of 1,200, although Colorado is the outlier, allowing systems of up to 1,920 watts, according to Bright Saver, a non-profit organization that sells plug-in solar kits.

UL 3700 safety certification is also required by most states, although Maine, New York and Vermont require that the inverter, panels, cables and mounting hardware all meet UL 3700 (or a comparable standard). According to Bright Saver, no vendor in the industry has achieved that yet.

UL 3700 was published in late 2025 and provides construction, performance and labeling criteria for plug-in solar systems. It is now the basis for UL Solutions’ safety testing and certification program for plug-in photovoltaic systems to which manufacturers can submit their systems for evaluation.

Products that meet the requirements are authorized to bear the UL 3700 mark.

“By defining how these systems must be built, evaluated for safety and safely installed, UL 3700 helps mitigate potential risks, and opens a path for more people to access resilient solar power,” said Ken Boyce, vice president, principal engineering, industrial testing, inspection and certification, at UL Solutions.

While plug-in solar is simple to install and use, the potential risk is when systems become overloaded and power may flow back into lines. In addition to defining safety standards for manufacturers, UL says the new standard requires features that mitigate accidental contact with hazardous electric parts, promote safe installation, protect against overloads and prevent electric current from flowing in the wrong direction.

UL describes in a white paper the three main hazards of plug-in solar systems and how they differ from traditional PV technology.

Overcurrent protection challenges: Branch circuits are designed for one-way power flow from the panelboard to the load. When a plug-in solar system backfeeds power into the same circuit, the combined current from the utility and plug-in solar source can exceed conductor ratings without tripping the circuit breaker. This undetected overload poses risks of fire and electric shock.

Touch safety hazards: Grid-interactive inverters used in plug-in solar systems are not evaluated for user contact safety. Accessible plug blades can become energized when exposed to sunlight, creating a shock hazard for consumers.

Ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) compatibility: Plug-in solar systems can compromise GFCI protection, a critical safety feature in outdoor and wet locations. Current GFCI standards assume unidirectional current flow, but plug-in solar introduces bidirectional flow, potentially blinding GFCIs and leaving circuits unprotected.

The advantages of plug-in solar are ease of installation and cost. In terms of ease of use, “they’re literally plug and play,” Stephan Scherer said in a recent webinar. Scherer is founder of Craftstrom a manufacturer of plug-in solar devices.

As for cost, Scherer said the cheapest systems can be purchased today for under $500. “It’s way more affordable than traditional solar, currently at about half to a third the cost of traditional solar, he said. Currently at about $1.50 per watt, Bright Saver anticipates prices to fall precipitously in the coming year.

Source: Bright Saver

Payback time, like traditional solar, depends on the electric rate and how much the system is producing, but typically the payback period is between two and six years in the U.S., Scherer said.

Together, these agreements further strengthen the long-standing partnership between ENGIE and QTS while expanding ENGIE’s renewable energy footprint in the ERCOT market.

QTS is a long-standing ENGIE customer, and this agreement reflects its continued work with ENGIE to support renewable energy solutions tailored to the evolving needs of the data center industry.

“This project is a meaningful step forward in our renewable energy strategy, supporting the long-term sustainability and operational resilience of our Texas footprint,” said Travis Wright, Vice President Energy and Sustainability, QTS.

“By partnering with ENGIE, we’re able to support reliable, renewable energy procurement while simplifying delivery through our retail supply arrangement. Collaborations like this help us align clean energy procurement with the operational needs of our data centers.”

“Data center customers continue to seek long-term, dependable renewable energy solutions that align with both operational and sustainability goals,” said Taymur Bunkheila, Regional Vice President, Key Accounts and Energy+, ENGIE North America. “ENGIE’s global experience and integrated capabilities enable us to structure customized solutions that seamlessly combine renewable generation with retail power supply.”

Lubio Solar is an approximately 61 MWac pre-commercial-operation-date solar project located in Kaufman County, Texas, developed by ABEI Energy. Once operational, the project is expected to generate approximately 150 GWh of clean electricity annually, equivalent to avoiding 100,778 metric tons of CO₂ emissions per year. This transaction marks ABEI Energy’s first renewable energy deal with ENGIE in the United States, building on an established partnership between the two companies in Europe.

ENGIE’s proven global leadership in renewable corporate PPAs reinforces its ability to deliver at this scale. Ranked first worldwide in BloombergNEF’s 2025 benchmark, with 3.6 GW signed in 2025 and 13.8 GW contracted since 2011, ENGIE holds the highest total globally over the 2011-2025 period, built on long-term partnerships with leading technology companies and a growing business-to-business customer base.

As data centers increase demand for renewable power across the United States, ENGIE continues to deliver integrated energy solutions that combine renewable generation, retail supply and energy management expertise. This three-party agreement demonstrates ENGIE’s ability to structure customized, scalable solutions that support the growing energy needs of the data center sector.

text:
Whose Movement Is It?, a series co-produced by NPQ and the Environmental Justice Oral History Project, is a call to action for those at the forefront of environmental justice decision-making, drawing on insights, hopes, and visions for the future from some of the foundational women organizers of the environmental justice movement.

In the autumn of 1982, residents organized inside Coley Springs Baptist Church in Warren County, NC, to stop the state from burying PCB-contaminated soil in their community. For six weeks, men, women, and children marched and lay down in the road in front of trucks hauling toxic waste. More than 500 people were arrested. It was from a jail cell in Warren County that the term “environmental racism” was first spoken aloud—not coined by a scientist or a policy office, but by the people living closest to the harm, organizing without institutional permission.

This year marks 250 years since a different group of people decided they, too, would no longer wait for permission from the institutions above them. As the country marks the semi-quincentennial of the Declaration of Independence, it’s worth remembering that the American experiment, like the environmental justice movement 206 years later, was built the same way: locally, informally, and with life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness in mind.

A Movement Built to Stay Local

Environmental justice was built on an understanding of the importance of locality and intentionality. The movement’s founders were not building a national institution; they were responding to what was poisoning their water, air, and children in the town where they lived. That hyperlocal character has sometimes been described as a weakness—a movement fractured into silos, unable to coordinate at scale. It’s a fair critique, but also an incomplete one. Decentralization is a large part of why the environmental justice movement has stayed effective where more institutionalized environmentalism has not. A community organization answers to the community it’s from; it cannot drift from its founding mission the way a large nonprofit can, because it has no distance to drift.

That principle has deep roots in the civil rights movement, which environmental justice grew out of, a movement whose most consequential victories rarely started with a national strategy. Four college students sitting down at a segregated Greensboro lunch counter in February 1960 had no mandate from any national organization. Within two months, tens of thousands of students in dozens of cities had staged sit-ins of their own, each one organized locally and stitched together only after the fact into something resembling a coordinated movement.

Decentralization is a large part of why the environmental justice movement has stayed effective where more institutionalized environmentalism has not.A few years earlier, a single woman refusing to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus became the spark for a year-long boycott sustained not by a citywide carpool network improvised block by block, church by church, and ride by ride. In both cases, the power came from the same place: a hyperlocal action specific enough to be immediately understandable on the ground and moving the needle enough that other communities recognized their own struggle in it and picked it up. Warren County would use that same mechanism, almost without realizing it, a generation later.

Hazel M. Johnson practiced that strategy without ever calling it a model. Living in the Altgeld Gardens public housing complex on Chicago’s South Side, surrounded by what she called a “toxic doughnut” of landfills and industrial polluters, Johnson founded People for Community Recovery in 1979—unpaid, unaffiliated with any national environmental organization, working block by block with her own neighbors. By 1991, delegates at the first National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit were calling her the “mother of environmental justice”—not the leader of a big green nonprofit, but a community ambassador and leader of her local tenant council.

The Role Institutions Must Play

None of this means institutions have no role. States can use the Clean Water Act to block a pipeline, as North Carolina and Virginia did to stop the Atlantic Coast Pipeline, the fight Donna Chavis spent years organizing as a Lumbee elder in Robeson County. Federal agencies can fund microgrids and community benefit plans, the way the Department of Energy did under Shalanda Baker’s direction before that framework was dismantled within weeks of a change in administration. Private developers can write community benefit agreements that keep clean energy investment from repeating the harms it claims to fix. Journalists can spend a year on one story, the way Jane Kay’s reporting on Tucson’s contaminated water gave Rose Marie Augustine’s community the exposure it needed to act. Even the largest environmental nonprofits can still choose to redirect funding and platform toward the organizations already doing the work.

State and federal government, the municipalities, the private sector, journalists and researchers who disseminate information, and the Big Green nonprofits that have spent a century building institutional power. The question asked of each one is the same: does this institution support community-led environmental justice work, or does the institution itself try to lead the work?

By 1991, delegates at the first National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit were calling her [Hazel M. Johnson] the “mother of environmental justice”—not the leader of a big green nonprofit, but a community ambassador and leader of her local tenant council.

The distinction matters more than it might seem. An institution that funds, amplifies, or defers to community leadership extends the movement’s reach without changing its shape. An institution that tries to run the movement risks doing what large institutions do by default: smoothing out the specificity that made the original organizing effective in the first place, replacing a tenant council’s urgency with a program office’s timeline. Big Greens’ own diversity numbers, which have declined for the first time on record in the years since they publicly pledged to do better, aren’t proof that institutions can’t help: They’re proof of what happens when an institution tries to hold the wheel instead of handing it back.

The Women Who Carried It

Nearly every pivot point in US environmental justice movement history was led by a woman whose name took decades to attach to the work.

In the spring of 1776, as her husband sat in Philadelphia debating the shape of the new nation, Abigail Adams wrote to ask that the new laws “remember the ladies” and not hand husbands the same unchecked power the colonies were fighting to escape from the Crown. It would be nearly a century and a half before the country followed through on that request.

Dollie Burwell and Angella Dunston represented an intergenerational coalition that organized the church basements and phone trees that got Warren County’s protesters into the streets. Vernice Miller-Travis mapped the geospatial data behind the 1987 Toxic Wastes and Race report that gave the movement its first hard evidence. Individuals like Pam Tau Lee, Susana Almanza, Peggy Shepard, and Dr. Mildred McClain were the conveners who established the 17 Principles of Environmental Justice that continue to undergird all best movement practice. Individuals like Leslie Fields, Rev. Susan Hendershot, and Queen Quet Marquetta L. Goodwine of the Gullah Geechee Nation have dedicated their careers to building institutions across policy, culture, and faith designed to serve all of us. None of them waited for a national office to tell them the work mattered.

Two hundred fifty years after a woman in Braintree, MA, asked to be remembered in the laws her husband was helping write, and more than 40 years after a jail cell in Warren County gave the environmental justice movement its name, the work record catches what was always true continues. This movement was built in kitchens, church basements, and tenant council meetings, by people—disproportionately women—who had no institution behind them and built one anyway. The stakeholders examined in the stories that follow all have something to offer to the work, but none of them are the work itself. That belongs, as it always has, to the communities doing it.

text:
LANSING, Mich. — The Trump administration has made clear its disdain for electric vehicles and clean energy. Yet at the grand opening of South Korea–based LG Energy Solution’s latest battery manufacturing facility, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum cheered the factory as a fulfillment of the president’s agenda.

“That’s the American energy dominance in action, which is more jobs, strong allies, secure supply chains — and right here, that’s happening,” Burgum said Tuesday during the Lansing factory’s opening ceremony.

LG executives have framed the plant’s opening in similar terms, echoing the administration’s focus on energy security and the importance of making the tech in the U.S., given that China produces most of the world’s batteries.

And like many of its peers in the industry, LG has adapted wide swaths of its Lansing site, originally meant only for EV batteries, to make what is proving to be a more politically palatable technology: energy storage systems for power grids.

“No matter which side of the aisle you’re on, there’s a desire to have energy independence and to meet load growth,” said Devon Wilson, vice president of sales and marketing for LG’s U.S. energy storage division.

LG invested more than $2 billion into building its new Lansing plant, which currently employs 900 people and plans to hire approximately 800 more.

Once at full capacity next year, the facility is expected to produce more than 35 gigawatt-hours of battery cells annually, according to Anthony O’Donovan, the plant’s operations director. That would make it one of the biggest domestic plants producing cells, which are the individual building blocks of battery systems, LG Energy Solution spokesperson Phil Lienert confirmed.

From Lansing, the cells will go to plants across the country — including both to clients and to one of LG’s own facilities in Holland, Michigan — to be connected together to form battery modules, which are then arranged into battery packs, Lienert said.

This domestic network of battery manufacturing is very new, and arriving just as battery energy storage systems themselves grow at a rapid clip. The U.S. didn’t make any of its own battery cells until 2025, when companies including LG added a total of 20 GWh of manufacturing capacity, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group.

By the end of this year, the coalition expects that figure to increase nearly fivefold, to 96 GWh of cell production capacity.

Diversifying beyond EVs

The Lansing facility was first announced in 2022 as part of Ultium Cells, a joint venture between LG and General Motors to source battery cells for the Michigan automaker’s EVs.

By 2024, however, consumer interest in EVs was lagging, and President Donald Trump vowed on the campaign trail to slash federal support for the vehicles. At the end of that year, GM sold its stake in the Lansing factory to LG, making the Korean company the site’s full owner.

The Trump administration has since eliminated the $7,500 tax credit for consumers who purchase EVs and canceled more than $700 million in federal funds for battery and EV manufacturing projects. (It did, however, preserve tax credits for clean energy manufacturing facilities and for the installation of stationary storage systems.)

By the end of 2025, dozens of battery and EV manufacturing projects were canceled nationwide, totaling more than $21 billion in lost investment, according to a report from E2, a clean energy advocacy group. Michigan, which had banked on exactly these types of projects to grow its economy, given its automotive prowess, was hit the hardest.

So, LG leaders decided to embrace a more promising sector: energy storage.

In the last few years, energy demand in the U.S. has surged in part because of the massive data centers being built for the artificial intelligence boom. Battery storage systems are well-positioned not only to swiftly meet tech companies’ demand for power, but also to absorb the sharp dips and spikes in energy usage inherent to AI data centers, Wilson said.

“It’s a great situation for us,” Wilson said. ​“We’ve seen an explosion in the size of the ESS [energy storage system] market, so we’ve really been able to grow our demand.”

In just four years, the amount of battery storage capacity in the U.S. has increased nearly tenfold, from 4.7 gigawatts in 2021 to 43.6 gigawatts at the end of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

This year, developers have already built 8.2 gigawatts of battery storage nationwide, according to the EIA — a statistic that Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a prominent Democrat, hailed as ​“amazing” at the opening of LG’s Lansing factory.

She also referenced Michigan’s ​“historic clean energy law” that requires 2.5 gigawatts of battery storage, which are often installed alongside solar farms to help stretch the carbon-free energy into other times of the day, by 2030.

“Michigan is poised to take advantage of this growth,” Whitmer said.

From one customer to many

In line with market shifts, the Lansing plant has diversified so that it will produce roughly half EV battery cells and half energy storage cells, according to Bob Lee, the North American president of LG Energy Solution.

The EV battery cells will no longer go to GM, but to Toyota. And the plant will produce nickel-manganese-cobalt cells, which are more energy-dense, according to LG’s press release.

Meanwhile, the energy storage cells have been contracted by a variety of offtakers, including renewable-project developer Terra-Gen and Korean clean energy manufacturer Qcells, LG spokesperson Lienert said. These cells will be lithium-iron phosphate, which isn’t as energy-dense as other chemistries but has less of a fire risk.

Next year, as the Lansing facility ramps up, it is also expected to supply Tesla’s Megapack 3 factory in Houston, an agreement that Lienert confirmed but would not elaborate on.

First reported by Reuters last summer, the $4.3 billion LG-Tesla deal was officially announced in March — but by the Trump administration as part of its focus on energy security, not by the companies.

Now that it’s up and running, the Lansing facility joins LG’s growing portfolio of cell manufacturing sites. The Korean company still runs two Ultium EV battery plants with GM, one in Tennessee, another in Ohio.

Last year, LG expanded its flagship Michigan site in Holland, which in 2012 became the first in the U.S. to make EV batteries, to also produce energy storage battery cells and packs.

General Motors spent the past several years preparing its Lansing operations for an electric future. Now that strategy has changed, and hundreds of workers are temporarily losing their jobs while the automaker prepares the plant for a very different kind of vehicle.

GM plans to lay off roughly 350 employees at its Lansing Grand River Assembly/Stamping and Lansing Regional Stamping facilities beginning January 14, 2027. The downtime is connected to retooling for a new internal-combustion Cadillac sedan rather than the electric vehicles once planned for the site.

The layoffs are expected to be temporary. According to Automotive News, GM intends to recall the affected workers after the retooling work is completed, while the UAW contract with the automaker will allow them to receive 74 percent of their regular hourly wages during the layoff.

It's a notable reversal for a facility that GM previously positioned as part of its expanding U.S. EV manufacturing footprint. The company announced a $1.25 billion investment in Lansing in 2023, followed by a $500 million federal grant intended to support the conversion of the facility for electrified vehicle production.

Lansing Was Supposed To Become An EV Plant

GM's original plan placed Lansing alongside several other factories being prepared for electric vehicle production. Those included Factory Zero in Detroit-Hamtramck, Orion Assembly in Michigan, Spring Hill Manufacturing in Tennessee, and Fairfax Assembly in Kansas.

The Lansing investment became even more significant in 2024 when GM was selected to receive $500 million from the U.S. Department of Energy. The federal funding was intended to help convert the facility for production of electrified vehicles while preserving manufacturing employment.

Those plans were drawn up during a period when automakers were expecting EV adoption to accelerate considerably faster. The industry has since adjusted production plans and investments as demand developed differently from some earlier projections.

GM has been among the companies recalibrating its strategy. Rather than dedicating Lansing exclusively to its electric ambitions, the automaker is now preparing the facility to produce another generation of combustion-powered vehicles.

A New Cadillac Sedan Is Coming Instead

The vehicle expected to emerge from the retooled Lansing operation is a new Cadillac sedan, widely believed to be the next-generation CT5. Reports indicate it will use an updated version of GM's rear-wheel-drive Alpha architecture.

title: Global EV Sales Reach 27% Share in 2026 - Design News
description:
BloombergNEF’s annual Electric Vehicle Outlook (EVO) predicts that more than a quarter (27%) of cars sold globally in 2026 will be electric.
Unsurprisingly, China leads the way in EV adoption, accounting for the largest share of the global EV market.
Chinese EV manufacturers lead sales in Thailand, while Vietnam’s domestic producer Vinfast accounted for virtually all EV sales there.
While EV sales continue to grow, slowdowns in the US and China are still flattening the global sales growth curve.
Global electric generation for EVs will need to grow from 367 terawatt-hours in 2025 to an eye-popping 2,700 TWh by 2040.
text:
Despite US market turbulence from the discontinuation of federal tax credits and supply disruptions caused by on-again, off-again tariffs, electric vehicle adoption continues to grow, according to a new report from BloombergNEF.

BloombergNEF’s annual Electric Vehicle Outlook (EVO) predicts that more than a quarter (27%) of cars sold globally in 2026 will be electric. That is up from 9% five years ago, and more than half (52%) of all passenger vehicles sold worldwide will be electric by 2035.

The value story of EV ownership is driving the increase, as lithium-ion battery prices fall, more affordable EV models are introduced, and EV adoption in emerging markets booms. Rising prices for gasoline and diesel are additional drivers, the report points out.

Unsurprisingly, China leads the way in EV adoption, accounting for the largest share of the global EV market. At the same time, emerging EV markets show increasing demand for EVs, with adoption now exceeding that of the US.

Look at Singapore, where nearly half of all new cars sold last year were electric, Vietnam, with 39% EV market share, and Thailand at 27%. Chinese EV manufacturers lead sales in Thailand, while Vietnam’s domestic producer Vinfast accounted for virtually all EV sales there.

BloombergNEF predicts that the global EV shift will finally start cutting into petroleum demand by 2029, with road transport use of gasoline and diesel declining after that.

While EV sales continue to grow, slowdowns in the US and China are still flattening the global sales growth curve. In the US, for example, EV sales are down 19% this year because of the cancellation of government support for EVs and the vehicle sales that were pulled ahead to 2025 in anticipation of that.

These policies will slow US EV adoption enough that the fleet on the road in 2040 will still only be 24% EVs, BloombergNEF forecasts. “While EV adoption continues to advance globally, the pace of the transition is becoming increasingly uneven across markets, driven largely by policy changes in the US and a maturing market in China,” said Aleksandra O’Donovan, Head of Electric Vehicles at BloombergNEF.

“In spite of the unevenness, it is encouraging to see that the longer-term trend towards electrification remains intact, driven by improving vehicle economics, falling battery costs, and rapid adoption across emerging markets,” she added.

In European markets, the report found that the cost premium for EVs compared to combustion-powered vehicles was cut in half, dropping from 34% more for EVs to just 17% more in 2024. Battery cost continues to be the driver of the cost difference between the vehicle types, with China’s industry enjoying a significant advantage.

“China continues to benefit from a mature manufacturing supply chain, lower input costs, favorable financing conditions, and intense competition, resulting in the world’s lowest EV battery prices,” the report states. “Differences in manufacturing scale and supply-chain integration with regions like North America and Europe mean higher prices are likely to persist.”

The researchers concluded that it will take until 2047 before the majority of passenger vehicles on the road globally are electric.

“Slow fleet replacement rates in many markets mean that there are still a lot of combustion vehicles on the global road in the long-term, creating a headache for policymakers aiming for net-zero transport,” said Andrew Grant, Head of Intelligent Mobility at BloombergNEF.

“That said, even meeting the demands of the electric vehicles that our outlook sees on the road creates plentiful opportunities, including roughly $2.2 trillion in spending per year on vehicles alone by 2035, and another $524 billion in investment in the required charging infrastructure between now and 2035.”

Another headwind for EV adoption is the electricity needed to power them and the competition for that electricity from data centers. Global electric generation for EVs will need to grow from 367 terawatt-hours in 2025 to an eye-popping 2,700 TWh by 2040.

title: Anthro Energy breaks ground on $45M Kentucky factory to feed US battery supply chain
description:
Anthro Energy broke ground Tuesday on a Louisville, Kentucky, factory that can produce enough electrolyte for more than 300,000 electric vehicles.
Battery makers are racing to secure materials free of "foreign entity of concern" restrictions — supply not controlled by Chinese companies.
The startup, which raised its first funding round four years ago, wants the factory to anchor the emerging US battery supply chain.
"Within a 12-hour drive, you can get to 70% of the battery production facilities in the United States that exist today," said co-founder and chief executive officer David Mackanic.
Solid-state batteries have yet to reach their potential because no one has cost-effectively manufactured durable cells at scale.
text:
What's the deal? Anthro Energy broke ground Tuesday on a Louisville, Kentucky, factory that can produce enough electrolyte for more than 300,000 electric vehicles. The plant will make 25 gigawatt-hours' worth of electrolytes annually and is scheduled to start production in 2028.

Why now? Battery makers are racing to secure materials free of "foreign entity of concern" restrictions — supply not controlled by Chinese companies. Anthro wants its factory to fill that gap for US customers.

What's the endgame? The startup, which raised its first funding round four years ago, wants the factory to anchor the emerging US battery supply chain. "Within a 12-hour drive, you can get to 70% of the battery production facilities in the United States that exist today," said co-founder and chief executive officer David Mackanic.

To build it, Anthro secured a $24.9 million award from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and $18.4 million in investment tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act. Kentucky added $2.3 million in tax incentives in exchange for 110 permanent jobs.

The product: The factory will make a range of electrolytes, but Mackanic wants much of its output eventually dedicated to Anthro's own polymer, Proteus. It flows into a cell as a liquid, then firms up to glue the anode and cathode together — a design meant to pave the way to solid- and semi-solid-state batteries. The result, he said, is a cell "10 to 15 times stronger than with a liquid electrolyte" that can also flex.

Solid-state batteries promise higher energy density and lower fire risk by removing flammable electrolytes, and their solid barrier blocks dendrites — spiky growths that can short-circuit cells. Chinese companies are reportedly targeting trial production of solid-state batteries in 2027.

What could go wrong? Solid-state batteries have yet to reach their potential because no one has cost-effectively manufactured durable cells at scale. Many battery materials companies have failed at exactly this point, scaling from small to large production.

The signal: With federal funding behind it, Anthro is betting a domestic, China-free electrolyte source can clear the industry's "valley of death" — and put US solid-state batteries within reach for EVs, drones, and robots.
