Clean Energy Broadens Its Base Clean energy manufacturing should no longer be viewed as a niche industry.
text:
By Anne Cosgrove

From the July / August 2026 Issue

The clean energy manufacturing sector has evolved beyond a collection of individual factories producing solar panels, wind turbine components, or battery cells. Rather than evaluating a single manufacturing operation in isolation, companies are now considering where an entire network of suppliers, logistics providers, utilities, research institutions, and skilled labor can support long-term growth.

The American Clean Power Association’s (ACP) “America Builds Power: The State of Clean Energy Manufacturing” 2026 report illustrates how significant the sector has become. According to ACP, more than 825 clean energy manufacturing facilities now operate across all 50 states, with 70 new facilities opening during 2025. The industry contributes approximately $31 billion annually to U.S. GDP, supports 216,000 manufacturing jobs, and is projected to exceed 950 manufacturing facilities employing roughly 374,000 workers by 2030.

An Industry Becoming An Industrial Ecosystem

What distinguishes today’s clean energy manufacturing sector is the increasing depth of domestic supply chains. Earlier investments often focused on final assembly—solar module plants, wind tower fabrication, or battery pack assembly. Today’s projects encompass nearly every stage of production, from processed battery materials and electrical steel to transformers, inverters, nacelles, power electronics, cables, structural components, and advanced grid technologies.

In its report released in May 2026, ACP identified more than 300 U.S. factories producing core clean energy components, including wind blades, towers, nacelles, solar modules, and battery products. Domestic manufacturing capacity is now sufficient to meet U.S. demand for several major products, including solar modules, battery modules, wind towers, and wind nacelles.

Expanding Supplier Base Changes Site Selection Approach

As manufacturers seek locations where suppliers are nearby, transportation costs can be reduced, inventory requirements minimized, and production schedules coordinated more efficiently, the site selection approach takes a new lens. The clustering effect also creates advantages for suppliers themselves, who gain access to multiple customers within a concentrated geography.

While batteries production continues to attract significant investment, the clean energy manufacturing landscape overall has become more diversified. Major investment activity now includes for example:

Solar modules, cells, trackers

Battery cells, battery modules, and battery materials

Wind blades and towers

Electrical transformers

High-voltage switchgear

Transmission equipment

Grid modernization technologies

Power electronics

Energy storage systems

Electrical components, supporting data centers and industrial electrification

The increasing emphasis on transformers and grid equipment is particularly noteworthy. As utilities work to accommodate growing electricity demand from manufacturing, AI data centers, and electrification, bottlenecks in transmission infrastructure have elevated these products from supporting equipment to strategic manufacturing assets.

Similarly, suppliers producing electrical equipment, structural steel, precision castings, composites, industrial automation systems, and specialty materials are increasingly becoming part of the broader clean energy manufacturing ecosystem.

Rather than serving a single technology, many suppliers now support multiple industries simultaneously.

Infrastructure Requirements

Many clean energy manufacturing projects require infrastructure that differs substantially from conventional industrial operations.

Electricity availability has become one of the primary differentiators. Battery manufacturing, advanced materials processing, polysilicon production, and other energy-intensive operations require large quantities of reliable electric service with opportunities for future expansion. Increasingly, manufacturers are evaluating not simply today’s available capacity but whether utilities can support future phases of growth.

Power quality also matters. Many advanced manufacturing processes require stable voltage, redundant electrical feeds, and minimal service interruptions to avoid costly production disruptions.

Transportation infrastructure remains equally important. Oversized wind turbine components require specialized highway access, while battery materials often depend on efficient rail service and intermodal connections. Ports continue to play an important role for manufacturers importing raw materials or exporting finished products.

According the American Clean Power Association in its second annual “State of Clean Energy Manufacturing” report, 70 new clean energy manufacturing facilities came online in the U.S. in 2025 (see map above). This brought the total to more than 825 facilities across all 50 states (see map below). (Images courtesy of American Clean Power Association)

Workforce Is Becoming More Specialized

Although clean energy manufacturing creates substantial employment, companies increasingly emphasize workforce quality over sheer labor availability.

The ACP report shares that clean energy factory workers earn approximately 35% more than the average American worker, reflecting the industry’s demand for advanced technical skills.

The overlap with automotive, aerospace, semiconductor, and advanced materials manufacturing has intensified competition for talent. As a result, partnerships with community colleges, technical schools, universities, apprenticeship programs, and customized workforce training initiatives increasingly influence location decisions.

Geography Reflects Manufacturing Ecosystems

The ACP report highlights particularly large concentrations of facilities in Texas, Tennessee, Georgia, Ohio, and North Carolina. Beyond these established clusters, additional regions continue gaining momentum. Parts of the Midwest are leveraging existing industrial capabilities in steel, machinery, and automotive manufacturing, while portions of the Southeast continue attracting suppliers that wish to locate near rapidly expanding assembly operations.

While the United States has seen a surge of clean energy manufacturing tied to domestic supply chain expansion, Canada is carving out its own role by leveraging abundant clean electricity, critical minerals, and integrated North American supply chains. Canada is developing regional centers of excellence where natural resources, industrial expertise, and energy infrastructure align.

Canada’s value proposition may begin with electricity. Approximately 80% of the country’s electricity generation comes from non-emitting sources—including hydroelectric, nuclear, wind, and solar—providing manufacturers with access to reliable, low-carbon power that is increasingly important for both operating costs and corporate sustainability goals. Federal investment tax credits, provincial incentive programs, and a growing emphasis on transmission expansion further strengthen Canada’s role in the growth of energy-intensive manufacturing, including clean energy.

Similar to trends identified in ACP’s analysis of U.S. manufacturing, Canadian provinces are seeking to attract not only large manufacturing plants but also suppliers, component manufacturers, logistics providers, research institutions, and workforce training partners.

Clean Energy Broadens Its Base

Clean energy manufacturing should no longer be viewed as a niche industry. It has become a broad manufacturing platform encompassing hundreds of facilities, a growing number of suppliers, and advanced technologies. The industry’s continued growth depends not simply on available land or incentive packages, but on the ability of locations to provide resilient infrastructure, reliable electricity, skilled workers, integrated supply chains, and development-ready sites.

As clean energy manufacturing continues to mature, successful projects will be driven by a more comprehensive evaluation of the entire industrial ecosystem surrounding a site—not just the individual facility.

title: We need to press Big Tech on their AI partnerships with Big Oil
description:
And yet, Microsoft, Google and Amazon have all created custom AI or machine-learning tools for fossil fuel companies to help them increase production.
Remember: In the scenarios the researchers modeled, global emissions fell only when AI produced no productivity gains for the fossil fuel industry.
On Tuesday, I emailed the press teams at Microsoft, Google and Amazon to ask them to respond to the research.
The other reason I’m telling you this is because I realized that simply making people aware of the problem of enabled AI emissions is not enough.
One obvious solution is for these tech companies to stop making custom AI tools for the fossil fuel industry.
text:
Lots of people—way more than usual!—are reading and sharing last week’s article about a new study finding that Big Oil’s use of AI to increase production could trigger 3.3 to 13.3 times more climate pollution than the emissions from AI data centers.

The attention is promising. As the study authors told us, expanding the climate conversation about AI beyond data centers to include “enabled emissions” is the necessary first step toward making sure AI doesn’t lock us into dangerous, irreversible warming.

But despite all this reaction, I’m not seeing many people ask what I believe to be the most important question raised by the research:

Why are these huge technology companies making custom AI tools to help the fossil fuel industry produce more oil and gas in the first place?

Microsoft, Google and Amazon have all promised both to fight climate change and to develop AI responsibly. Microsoft says it will become carbon negative by 2030, and that the systems it builds “must also support the long-term health of the planet.” Google says its AI safeguards are designed to mitigate “unintended or harmful outcomes,” and it aims to reach net zero emissions across its operations and value chain by 2030. Amazon says responsible AI includes preventing harmful outputs and misuse, and it has pledged to reach net zero carbon by 2040.

And yet, Microsoft, Google and Amazon have all created custom AI or machine-learning tools for fossil fuel companies to help them increase production. So how are these companies going to respond to research suggesting their actions are achieving the exact opposite of what they promise?

Remember: In the scenarios the researchers modeled, global emissions fell only when AI produced no productivity gains for the fossil fuel industry. It was not enough for AI to help renewable energy, too.

So do Microsoft, Google and Amazon accept that finding? And if so, what are they going to do about it?

I think these are the most important accountability questions that can be asked about this issue right now. So I’m trying to get answers. On Tuesday, I emailed the press teams at Microsoft, Google and Amazon to ask them to respond to the research. In essence, I asked whether they accept the study’s findings; how their work increasing fossil fuel production aligns with their climate and responsible-AI commitments; whether they track or disclose the emissions their technology enables; and whether the findings will prompt them to stop making custom AI tools that help fossil fuel companies produce more.

One thing I expect to hear from these companies is that their AI technology is actually helping oil companies reduce the emissions intensity of their operations. But emissions intensity is not the same thing as overall emissions. AI may help an oil company emit less pollution per barrel of oil. But if the company is producing more barrels than it otherwise would have, total emissions can still rise. That’s why I specifically asked the tech companies whether they’re looking at the whole picture: not just whether AI makes each barrel cleaner to produce, but whether it helps produce more barrels overall.

Now, why am I telling you this? Admittedly, it’s not common practice for reporters to tell their audiences about questions they’ve asked corporations before receiving answers. But I’m doing it because I think it might increase our chances of getting a response.

These days, it has become excruciatingly common practice for companies to ignore reporter requests, particularly when it comes to climate change. I’m hoping that knowing people are watching will inspire Microsoft, Google and Amazon to actually participate in the discussion.

I’m genuinely hoping these companies will take the research seriously, take our inquiry seriously, and provide thoughtful answers. Assuming they will, I’ve given them what I think is a reasonable amount of time to look into everything: A deadline of midday on August 25.

For what it’s worth, a Microsoft media relations representative swiftly responded to confirm receipt. Google also sent an automated confirmation. Amazon has not yet responded to confirm they got the questions, but that’s not always common practice.

The other reason I’m telling you this is because I realized that simply making people aware of the problem of enabled AI emissions is not enough. People also have to know what the solutions are in order to effectively demand change.

One obvious solution is for these tech companies to stop making custom AI tools for the fossil fuel industry. Another is for them to voluntarily track and disclose the emissions their technology enables—and count those emissions when making claims about their climate progress.

If they don’t do those things voluntarily, governments could step in. They could require enabled emissions disclosure, and place limits on AI applications designed to expand fossil fuel extraction. (The study found that carbon pricing alone, even at an extremely high level, reduced but did not reverse the emissions increase. Some direct constraint on AI-enabled fossil fuel expansion would still be necessary).

But if Microsoft, Amazon and Google are truly the climate champions they claim to be, they shouldn’t need to be forced.

I look forward to updating you next week after we get answers. And if we don’t, that will be a story in itself.

Other stories I'm following:

The Trump administration is officially opening untouched national forests to logging. On Tuesday, the Trump administration moved to roll back an environmental rule that blocks road construction, logging, and mining on tens of millions of acres of public forest land. While Trump is framing the move as necessary to control wildfires, as we’ve previously reported, that’s a scam! This is a brazen giveaway to the logging industry that, if anything, will worsen wildfires.

Data center gas plants will boost U.S. power emissions by 20 percent. This is why it’s still necessary to talk about the climate impact of data centers, via Bloomberg:

Data center developers are turning to bespoke natural-gas power plants, a development that promises to dramatically increase carbon emissions and make it harder for US technology companies to meet their lofty climate goals.

Ninety-nine proposed plants tracked by BloombergNEF would emit about 318 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually if run at industry-standard rates, according to a Bloomberg News analysis. The entire US electric power industry emitted about 1,485 million metric tons of carbon last year, according to Energy Information Administration data, meaning one slice of data center infrastructure has the potential to lift US power sector emissions by 20%, and as much as a third should the new plants run flat out.

Extreme heat more dangerous for people 60 and over than previously thought. From the Guardian:

Older adults will bear the brunt of increasingly frequent sustained spells of extreme heat globally as the world continues to warm up, according to a study in The Lancet Planetary Health. …

“Our results suggest accounting for age-stratified vulnerability, intolerable heat will be experienced at much larger scales and for longer durations, affecting far more people than previously thought,” according to the study, which was led by health academics from Stanford University in California.

Older adults are known to be more in danger because of the effects of very high temperatures. They sweat less, their hearts work harder in the heat and their blood vessels are less able to widen, limiting their capacity to stay cool.

…The study suggested older adults were “at risk of harmful and potentially fatal heat stress” at just 1.5C of warming above preindustrial levels, compared with 4C for younger adults.

Some personal news…

It’s been a busy last few days over in my household, for the most exciting reason: We have a new family member!

Margaritaville—Margo for short—came home with us on Friday from the Brandywine Valley SPCA. She’s a one-year-old pitbull mix (we think?) who loves everything and everyone, but especially Mr. Possum.

Five days in, we’re already in love—and Margo doesn’t seem to mind us, either. Stay tuned for more pics soon. (That’s the point of having a dog after all, right?)

title: Judge set to vaporize EPA bid to end California emissions standards - Courthouse News
description:
When Congress passed the Clean Air Act in 1967, California faced significant air quality and pollution problems that the federal emission standards were unlikely to address.
However, at that time, California was the only state with its own vehicle emission standards and its regulations had helped craft federal law.
Stander pointed to the Clean Air Act itself, which channels to the appellate courts.
Howell noted a stark difference in the length of procedural review under the Congressional Review Act and the normal legislative process, with the latter requiring many more steps.

text:
WASHINGTON (CN) — A federal judge on Wednesday signaled she’s likely to block the Environmental Protection Agency’s effort to nullify California’s Clean Air Act waivers, which allow the state to enact stricter emissions standards than the federal government.

Senior U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell expressed concern over the Justice Department’s position that any agency could effectively enlist Congress to undo longstanding regulations by reclassifying them as final rules and employing an expedited review process under the Congressional Review Act, a plan specifically laid out in the controversial Project 2025.

The exception at issue, known as the California waiver, was enacted in 1970s to address the dangerous levels of smog in Los Angeles and throughout the Golden State. It has since evolved to make the state a “laboratory of innovation” where automakers can test new technology.

When Congress passed the Clean Air Act in 1967, California faced significant air quality and pollution problems that the federal emission standards were unlikely to address. However, at that time, California was the only state with its own vehicle emission standards and its regulations had helped craft federal law.

Taking both California’s unique situation and automakers’ concerns about a patchwork system of emission standards across all 50 states, Congress created the California waiver directly in the Clean Air Act, balancing both issues.

Howell, a Barack Obama appointee, heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by California on June 22, seeking a preliminary injunction to order the EPA to withdraw its reclassification of waivers from 2009, 2013, 2022 and 2024 that put them up for congressional review.

Margaret Meckenstock with the California Attorney General’s Office argued Wednesday that Congress never would have passed the Congressional Review Act if it allowed executive agencies to suddenly change adjudicatory orders into final rules, and vice-versa.

If the statute is interpreted as going that far, it would “write the EPA out of the U.S. Code,” Meckenstock said.

Howell described the government’s position as seeming to allow any agency to “willy-nilly decide what’s a rule and what isn’t,” adding that this process opened the door to private interests — such as the American Petroleum Institute and the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufactures, which intervened in this case — to push such deregulation.

Justice Department attorney Robert Stander argued California had no avenue to challenge the EPA’s action of providing a report to Congress suggesting the waivers should be reclassified, and had no cause until lawmakers issued a joint resolution of disapproval that would then invalidate the rule.

Further, the state had brought its challenge in the wrong court, suggesting instead it would have to wait until Congress acts to challenge the decision in the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals — where the state currently has a pending challenge to the waiver reclassification as of Aug. 11. Stander pointed to the Clean Air Act itself, which channels to the appellate courts.

Howell noted a stark difference in the length of procedural review under the Congressional Review Act and the normal legislative process, with the latter requiring many more steps.

According to the Environmental & Energy Law Program at Harvard Law, the use of the Congressional Review Act increased dramatically in 2025. Before the past year, Congress had only used the statute once before 2017, 16 times in 2017 and three times in 2021. In 2025, Congress used it 22 times.

According to California, if the EPA’s reclassifications are ultimately upheld and the waivers can be considered rules subject to congressional review, the agency will have “eviscerated” the state’s right to contest further revocations.

The Trump administration revoked the exception in 2019 as part of its wide-reaching rollback of efforts to fight climate change. Then-EPA Administrator Andrew Wheeler said the rule worked against the idea of federalism by allowing a single state to dictate standards for the nation.

President Joe Biden reinstated the rule in March 2022. A group of red states and fuel industry groups then sued in May 2022 challenging the rule.

In September 2022, the California Air Resources Board passed a new set of regulations that essentially require all vehicles sold in the state to be either electric, hydrogen-fueled or at least plug-in hybrid by 2035. Soon after, 17 states adopted similar rules.

In April 2024, D.C. Circuit panel unanimously rejected an effort by 17 red states and fuel industry groups seeking to overturn the California waiver. The panel found that so long as California’s emission standards are at least as protective as federal regulations, the Clean Air Act requires the EPA to affirm them, unless they are deemed unnecessary or otherwise problematic.

“In other words, the federal regulations continue to act as the floor for emissions regulations, but California can seek to enact its own more stringent regulatory program above those federal requirements,” the panel wrote.

In December 2024, the Supreme Court rejected the states’ appeal and upheld the D.C. Circuit ruling.

text:
Electric vehicle and clean energy company Tesla is considering building a new $10.1 billion solar cell manufacturing facility in Fort Bend County, according to documents filed with the Texas Comptroller’s Office.

If approved, the plant, called Project Sun City, would be located on a 3,050-acre site off FM 762 and FM 1994 in Richmond, Texas. Tesla aims to finish construction in 2028, with the plant being operational by early 2029.

The plant will manufacture photovoltaic (PV) solar cells and modules that can convert sunlight into electricity. PV Magazine reports that the facility is "the largest single manufacturing investment Tesla has proposed on paper."

Advisory and consulting firm Kroll submitted the documents to the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts and noted if an agreement regarding tax incentives isn't reached, the project will exit Texas.

Tesla has requested credits under the Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation (JETI) Act. The incentive program aims to attract large, capital-intensive economic development projects by lowering the property taxes an entity must pay over 10 years if it meets requirements related to job creation and investment. For example, pharmaceutical giant Bristol Myers Squibb Co. recently announced that its forthcoming $2.3 billion Houston-area manufacturing site is a qualified project under the JETI program.

Kroll predicts that the facility would create 9,712 new full-time jobs, over 1,100 construction jobs and billions of dollars in future property tax revenue, the documents show. Additionally, it says the project will spur $1.1 billion in local business expenditures and that Texas would increase its GDP by approximately $107 billion as a result of the project activities.

Tesla opened its $200 million Megafactory in Brookshire, Texas, last year. The company is continuing its goal to deploy 100 gigawatts of solar manufacturing in the U.S before the end of 2028. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, 100 gigawatts is equal to about 8 percent of the country's power grid capacity.

text:
In the second quarter, U.S. companies announced nearly $8 billion in clean energy manufacturing investments, according to a new report from the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy.

However, while private-sector demand remains strong even as recent federal policy changes slow the sector’s growth, the report found that policy changes have contributed to nearly $40 billion in canceled investments and 53,000 manufacturing jobs since the beginning of 2025.

The report, called the State of Clean Energy Manufacturing, comes at the fourth anniversary of the Inflation Reduction Act, the single largest investment in climate and energy in American history. The report underscores both the law’s success in attracting private investment and the threat recent policy changes pose to that momentum.

“Four years after the Inflation Reduction Act helped launch a clean energy manufacturing boom, this report shows that companies see what the Trump administration refuses to acknowledge: clean energy technologies are cost-competitive and here to stay,” Grace Hauser, technical analyst, clean power at Environmental Defense Fund, said. “Federal policies that provide long-term certainty can keep that momentum going, but recent policy changes are putting America’s manufacturing competitiveness at risk.”

In Q2, companies announced $7.9 billion in new manufacturing investments while canceling $2.9 billion in previously announced projects. This resulted in $5 billion in net new investment. Solar manufacturing, transmission, and grid equipment drove the quarter’s growth. One of the biggest projects was Convalt Energy’s planned $5 billion solar manufacturing campus in New Mexico. It is the largest clean energy manufacturing investment announced since the start of the current administration.

However, Convalt’s project is only the third clean energy manufacturing investment of more than $1 billion announced in the past 18 months. In the previous 18-month period, from July 2023 through December 2024, companies announced 24 projects exceeding $1 billion.

Among the report’s key findings, companies announced 5,900 new manufacturing jobs in Q2 2026, while 2,800 previously announced jobs were canceled. The canceled jobs were primarily in electric vehicle, hydrogen electrolyzer and solar manufacturing.

Also, since the beginning of 2025, companies have canceled $39.6 billion in planned clean energy manufacturing investments and 53,400 announced manufacturing jobs.

Since 2000, companies have announced $244.8 billion in clean energy manufacturing investments and 331,900 manufacturing jobs, with more than 760 facilities operating or under construction nationwide.

Finally, since 2000, more than 70 percent of announced clean energy manufacturing investment has occurred in congressional districts currently represented by Republicans.

text:
Grounded, the Detroit-based manufacturing and mobility company of modular electric vehicles, announced it has closed a $5 million seed round and is moving production into a 50,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Detroit. The expansion increases Grounded’s production capacity by 1,900% and will support the launch of a new vehicle-agnostic box platform that extends the company’s software-defined, modular vehicle architecture into a significantly larger commercial fleet market of both electric and internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, company officials said in a press release.

“This new facility is a turning point for Grounded,” said Sam Shapiro, founder and CEO of Grounded. “We built this company to bring smart, modular electric vehicles to the businesses and institutions that keep our cities running. With this expansion, we can finally build at the scale our fleet customers need and bring our platform to an entirely new class of commercial vehicles.”

$5M Seed Round Fuels Next-Generation Manufacturing

The seed round will fund three areas of expansion: standing up the box platform manufacturing line, including new tooling, equipment and R&D; building out the larger Detroit production facility; and growing the manufacturing, engineering and sales team responsible for scaling the company’s vehicle platform.

The new box line builds on the software-defined, modular architecture Grounded developed for its existing van-based vehicles. Its adaptive customization technology allows a common vehicle platform to be configured for a wide range of applications, giving fleet operators purpose-built vehicles without requiring Grounded to engineer an entirely new vehicle for every use case, the company said.

“The economy is moving onto wheels,” said Grounded chief product officer Nadia Meyer. “We’re seeing notable growth across food and beverage franchises, field operations, public safety and mobile healthcare. Our box platform embraces those use cases and speeds manufacturing to meet that demand and serve the sizable addressable market.”

Growing Fleet Adoption Across Industries

Grounded says that it is already putting its electric fleet vehicles to work across a diverse set of industries. Customers include Colgate, Nokia, Coffee Fellows, Wayne State University Medical, PetEvolution and Healthy Mothers Healthy Babies, with vehicles supporting applications ranging from mobile medical and dental services to food service and other field operations.

The expansion marks the next phase in Grounded’s evolution from an electric RV startup into a broader advanced manufacturing and fleet technology company. Grounded will continue building fully electric RVs for direct-to-consumer customers while increasing its focus on commercial and government fleets seeking to electrify operations without sacrificing the flexibility of purpose-built vehicles.

“Grounded is a company on the move, both literally and figuratively,” said Kevin Johnson, president and CEO of the Detroit Economic Growth Corporation. “This team emerged from Newlab with a bold idea and turned it into a business that now requires 50,000 square feet and 15 new jobs to support its growth. Our Retention Program made the connections that kept this exciting company in the city, adding another strong chapter to Detroit’s story as a leader in mobility.”

Building the Team for the Next Stage of Growth

Grounded is also expanding its commercial leadership as it scales. The company has hired Drew Snow, formerly of Adrian Steel, as director of international sales to help grow the company’s fleet business and bring its modular electric vehicle platform to customers across new markets.

Grounded will begin production at the new Detroit facility in August 2026, with capacity ramping through 2027 to support existing commitments, the new box platform and a growing pipeline of enterprise and municipal fleet customers, the company said.

title: Judges reject waste sector challenge to EPA's PFAS hazardous designation
description:
Circuit Court of Appeals on Tuesday upheld the U.S. EPA’s designation of two PFAS chemicals as hazardous substances under CERCLA.
That decision refutes waste industry claims that the EPA overstepped its authority and unfairly exposed businesses to liability expenses.
The National Waste & Recycling Association and other groups, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, sued the EPA in 2024 over the designations.
The CERCLA hazardous designation was established during the Biden administration, but the EPA under the Trump administration said it would defend the rulemaking.
Judges also decided that the EPA had provided enough time to solicit public comments on the proposed CERCLA designation.
text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals on Tuesday upheld the U.S. EPA’s designation of two PFAS chemicals as hazardous substances under CERCLA. That decision refutes waste industry claims that the EPA overstepped its authority and unfairly exposed businesses to liability expenses.

The National Waste & Recycling Association and other groups, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, sued the EPA in 2024 over the designations. NWRA and the other petitioners say the EPA didn’t offer enough time for public comment on the matter and conducted a flawed cost-benefit analysis on the designation, among other claims.

The legal opinion, announced by a three-judge panel, affirms the EPA made a “reasoned decision” when designating PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act in 2024. The U.S. Chamber and NWRA have said they are considering next steps, but have not said whether they will appeal.

Dive Insight:

Although the EPA has made numerous PFAS-related decisions in recent years, the waste industry sees the CERCLA hazardous substance designation for the two per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances as having the most direct impact on operations. The waste industry has also benefitted in recent years from some PFAS management business opportunities.

NWRA considers waste operators as “passive receivers” that do not have control over PFAS-laden materials that enter their facilities, and believes the designation could lead to unintended consequences that might force landfills to reject PFAS-containing material, incur major costs for sorting or processing the material or face PFAS-related lawsuits.

Petitioners also include the American Chemistry Council, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, Associated General Contractors of America, the Recycled Materials Association, and American Forest & Paper Association.

Judges disagreed with that claim, saying the petitioners “have come forward with no evidence that those responsible for the presence of hazardous substances at a site have been unfairly saddled with liability or that the statute’s operation has hamstrung industry.”

In an emailed statement, NWRA President and CEO Michael E. Hoffman said the association was “disappointed” by the decision.

“While we support efforts to address PFAS contamination and protect public health and the environment, we remain concerned that this designation may create significant legal and financial uncertainty for passive receivers, including municipal solid waste landfills and other waste and recycling facilities that did not manufacture these chemicals but are responsible for managing materials generated throughout the economy.”

When NWRA, the U.S. Chamber and the other petitioners brought the case in 2024, they asked the judges to determine whether the EPA failed to provide “adequate notice and opportunity” to comment on the proposed rule and whether it offered an “adequate and reasonable explanation” for why it determined PFOA and PFOS should be designated as hazardous substances.

The CERCLA hazardous designation was established during the Biden administration, but the EPA under the Trump administration said it would defend the rulemaking.

In the ruling released on Tuesday, judges said the EPA offered numerous details as to why the two PFAS should be considered hazardous substances, noting that the agency spent pages of text describing possible health and developmental effects “including decreased infant birth weight and effects on fetuses during pregnancy; cardiovascular impacts like increased cholesterol in adolescents; increased liver enzymes, which can impact liver function; immunosuppression in adults and children” and other examples.

Judges also decided that the EPA had provided enough time to solicit public comments on the proposed CERCLA designation. “Petitioners’ members are seasoned participants in the highly regulated area of chemical substances’ commercial uses,” the judges wrote. “They were provided ample notice and opportunity to be heard through the notice and comment rulemaking process.”

NWRA, the U.S. Chamber and the other petitioners also argued that the EPA offered a flawed cost-benefit analysis on the impacts of the designation, saying EPA miscalculated cleanup costs at sites on the Superfund’s National Priorities List, ignored cleanup costs at federal sites and “failed to consider the impact of the Designation on small businesses.”

But judges said EPA’s analysis offered reasonable estimates for cleanup costs, and that an alternative cost model suggested by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce relied on outdated data and “discussions with industry rather than empirical data.”

In an emailed statement, Daryl Joseffer, president of the U.S. Chamber Litigation Center, said the group “respectfully disagree[s]” with the court’s decision.

“EPA’s failure to consider costs and consequences, as required by law, produced a deeply flawed rule that is more likely to spawn unnecessary, costly litigation than to drive expeditious, effective cleanup focused on actual risk,” Joseffer wrote. “Local governments, landowners, and businesses will now likely have to divert resources to fighting prolonged litigation battles — resources that could be used for more productive purposes, including cleanup.”

The judges’ decision does not change the wording or enforcement of the CERCLA hazardous substance designation for PFOS and PFOA, in part because that designation had never been suspended during the ongoing legal battle.

But waste industry groups are expected to continue seeking out additional protections against the possibility of liability issues under CERCLA.

The EPA under the Biden administration had previously stated that the hazardous substance designation was meant to hold polluters accountable for cleaning up certain PFAS and does not intend to pursue enforcement at certain types of landfills. Yet industry groups like NWRA have said the wording is not specific enough to protect them from potential negative impacts.

Taryn McKnight, vice president of product at Eurofins, an environmental testing company that offers PFAS-related testing services for a range of industries, said the EPA doesn’t have the authority to protect passive receivers from third-party claims. “Only Congress has that authority, and Congress has been debating for years whether to provide waivers to passive receivers,” she said.

NWRA and other groups have been asking Congress for a CERCLA exemption since at least 2022 due to such liability concerns. Some lawmakers have proposed related bills in past years, but none have progressed so far.

One of the latest moves is a proposed amendment to the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, proposed by Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska. It calls for exempting certain “resource management entities” from CERCLA liability related to PFAS releases from entities such as solid waste management and wastewater facilities.

“With this decision now, with the courts denying the petitioners’ request to review or overturn this ruling, that does put the pressure on Congress to make a decision and potentially provide those waivers,” McKnight said.

In the meantime, Hoffman stated that NWRA will continue “to advocate for policies that ensure that those most responsible for introducing PFAS into commerce bear primary responsibility for addressing contamination, while protecting critical waste and recycling infrastructure that communities rely on every day.”

text:
Collaboration Will Advance Research and Technical Insights Needed To Support Reliable, Resilient Energy Future for More Than 400 Million North Americans

The National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) announced a new partnership to advance the reliability of the North American bulk power system.

The organizations will work together to better understand how the power system is changing and identify new opportunities to keep electricity reliable and affordable.

“This partnership allows us to apply NLR research directly to the reliability challenges facing today’s grid,” said Kate Anderson, director of the Grid Planning and Analysis Center at NLR.

“By working alongside NERC, we can translate decades of U.S. Department of Energy investment in energy research into practical tools and insights that help keep the lights on for communities across North America,” added Bethany Frew, group manager for the Price Signals for Grid Services group at NLR.

The partnership will initially focus on integrating NERC’s high-resolution data, including more precise asset location information, into NLR’s grid-modeling capabilities. This will enable researchers to represent the power system in greater detail and support more sophisticated analysis of future reliability challenges.

The organizations expect the collaboration to inform new approaches to power system planning and reliability analysis across the industry.

“By combining NERC’s reliability expertise and NLR’s research capabilities, this partnership will allow us to enhance our organizations’ analytical capabilities, improve coordination on reliability research, and identify new opportunities to address future reliability challenges,” said John Moura, director of Reliability Assessments and Performance Analysis at NERC.

The partnership builds on a longstanding relationship between NLR and NERC researchers, including decades of collaboration through NERC events and a November 2025 visit that brought NERC and NLR grid-reliability researchers together to explore opportunities for deeper technical collaboration.

“Working with NERC has been one of the highlights of my time at the laboratory,” said Sinnott Murphy, an NLR grid researcher.

Surya Dhulipala, an NLR grid researcher, also said, "I'm particularly looking forward to the two-way exchange this partnership offers—contributing our hands-on experience with wide-area probabilistic assessments, while collaborating directly with the leading authority on grid reliability to help advance more robust, forward-looking resource adequacy methodologies across the industry."

NERC is a not-for-profit, international regulatory authority dedicated to effectively and efficiently reducing risks to the reliability and security of the bulk power system. NERC works with owners, operators, and consumers as well as federal, state, and provincial regulators across North America to develop and enforce mandatory reliability standards, monitor the grid, train personnel, and assess risks to ensure that the grid remains reliable and secure today and in the future.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Pennsylvania will give data center projects preferential permitting treatment if they commit to a set of power supply, environmental and cost-responsibility requirements under an executive order issued Tuesday by Gov. Josh Shapiro, D.

The state Department of Environmental Protection will develop the new review process. To receive a faster state permitting review, data center projects in Pennsylvania must source their electricity from new power supplies, including from growing amounts of firm clean power, according to the order, which affects proposals for projects with a peak demand of more than 25 MW.

The order “should further close the door” to the idea that independent power producers like Talen Energy, Vistra and PSEG Power will be able to sell power from their existing generating assets under long-term contracts to data centers in Pennsylvania, Jefferies equity analysts said in a note on Wednesday. However, Talen’s legacy deal to sell power from its majority-owned Susquehanna nuclear power plant to an Amazon data center appears safe, according to the note.

Dive Insight:

Shapiro’s executive order comes amid a wave of action by state and local governments aimed at setting limits on data center development. At least 81 cities and counties have moratoria on data center development, according to a National League of Cities database unveiled Wednesday.

Under the permitting framework set by the executive order, data center developers that sign a consent order and agreement requiring them to abide by the state’s infrastructure development standards unveiled in February will receive preferential treatment compared to those that don’t.

For example, applicants that execute a consent order and agreement will have their projects reviewed by DEP on a rolling basis, whereas for developers that don’t sign, the state won’t consider their applications until they have all local permits in hand as well as any needed water withdrawal or wastewater discharge authorizations.

“We have so much speculation in Pennsylvania — like, gold rush speculation on these data centers,” Katie Blume, political and legislative director for Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania, told Utility Dive in an interview. “A lot of this [order] is going to be weeding out those bad actors because they’re not going to want to spend five years in the permitting process.”

But Dan Diorio, executive vice president for state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, sounded a note of caution in an emailed statement.

“It’s important that rules are not changed midstream impacting ongoing investment in verified and responsible data center projects,” Diorio said. “Data centers take compliance and accountability seriously, building only where they are authorized to do so under local, state, and federal rules and regulations.”

The infrastructure development standards include requiring data centers to pay for “all costs caused in whole or in part by the interconnection, service, or load of a [data center] project, including any costs associated with energy and ancillary services, transmission, distribution, network upgrades.”

Besides requiring data centers to be supplied by new generating resources from the same local PJM Interconnection zone where the facilities are built, they must be supplied from growing amounts of firm clean energy such as solar, advanced nuclear and battery storage, Shapiro said when he signed the executive order.

The firm clean energy requirements ramp up from 10% on Jan. 1 to 14.5% three years later and 32% by Jan. 1, 2035.

The executive order directs the Pennsylvania DEP to expedite permitting for clean energy and storage facilities on brownfield sites. The DEP must also facilitate the use of advanced reconductoring and other advanced transmission technologies on existing transmission rights-of-way.

In prepared remarks, Shapiro pointed to the speed of data center development in the state, which he said has “seen an unacceptable number of speculative proposals ... many of them led by developers who have no regard for local communities.”

PPL Electric has about 20.7 GW of potential data center load with electric service agreements in Pennsylvania, according to an Aug. 7 investor presentation. FirstEnergy utilities in Pennsylvania have data center contracts totaling nearly 1 GW, the company said in a July 28 presentation.

It is unclear how those data center projects will be affected by the executive order, but slowing data center development could affect utility transmission spending in the state, the Jefferies analysts noted.

Exelon, FirstEnergy and PPL are “materially increasing their transmission investment with data center demand a key driver,” the analysts said. “If the pace of data center growth slows, we see downside pressure to the pace of transmission investments.”

Currently, data center-driven transmission costs are being shared with residential and other utility customers, they noted.

text:
LG Energy Solution has started battery production at a new 226-acre facility in Lansing, Michigan, bringing large-format battery manufacturing for electric vehicles and energy storage systems under one roof.

The plant is designed to reach more than 35 GWh of annual battery production at full scale and employ up to 1,700 people. The company has invested more than $2 billion in the Lansing facility since 2022 and currently employs about 900 people there.

The factory will make two types of lithium-ion batteries for different uses. Its lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) cells are intended for energy storage systems, while nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cells will supply Toyota for battery-electric vehicles. LFP batteries generally prioritize lower cost and longer cycle life, while NMC cells offer higher energy density, making each better suited to its intended application.

The LFP cells will be integrated by LG Energy Solution Vertech into complete storage systems for utility, grid-scale, commercial and industrial applications. NMC cells made at Lansing will power vehicles including the 2027 Toyota Highlander EV, which will be assembled in Kentucky.

Two battery types, one plant

The split production strategy gives the Lansing facility a role in both transportation and the electricity grid. Energy storage batteries can help utilities hold electricity and dispatch it when demand rises, while the automotive cells support a more localized U.S. battery supply chain.

More from Energy

See All

DTE Energy is expected to use batteries produced at Lansing for future energy storage projects. The company said domestic production will also help customers meet U.S. domestic content requirements.

“Today marks a defining milestone for LG Energy Solution. Lansing will produce advanced batteries that support not only the future of mobility, but also America’s growing energy infrastructure and digital economy,” said David Kim, CEO of LG Energy Solution.

“We are strengthening America’s battery ecosystem, expanding our manufacturing footprint and reaffirming our long-term commitment to the United States.”

The Lansing operation also expands LG Energy Solution’s manufacturing presence in Michigan. The company already operates a battery plant in Holland and maintains its North American regional headquarters and research and development facility in Troy.

Scaling North American storage

LG Energy Solution has invested more than $5 billion in Michigan since 2010. By the end of 2026, its Michigan workforce is expected to exceed 3,300 employees.

The company is also building a much larger North American footprint for energy storage batteries. It expects more than 50 GWh of total LFP cell-making capacity across North America by the end of 2026.

That capacity will come from three wholly owned plants and two joint ventures in the United States and Canada. The company expects about 80 percent of its global energy storage capacity to be located in North America by the end of this year.

For Lansing, the immediate focus is scaling production. Once fully operational, the facility will combine automotive battery manufacturing with cells destined for large-scale energy storage, giving Michigan another major role in the growing U.S. battery supply chain.

title: Texas welcomed data centers, now it's backtracking. It's time for a real plan
authors: The Dallas Morning News Editorial Board, Dallas Morning News Editorial
description:
Some opposition to data centers is NIMBYism, but parsing through people who don’t want any new development at all, some of the public’s anxiety surrounding data centers is warranted.
Advertisement Article continues below this ad Data centers represent a physical cost to the environment.
In addition to these physical manifestations, data centers are a symbol of technological intrusion into our lives and communities.
Although they have been around for at least a decade, it wasn’t until the artificial intelligence boom that the data center industry took off.
Greg Abbott was right to call for a pause on data centers, and it’s time to pivot.
text:
The cacophony surrounding data centers moving in across the state, many in largely rural areas, has grown almost as loud as the hum some residents are complaining about coming from their industrial neighbors.

In Red Oak, residents have had enough of the data centers that are no longer hidden away in the county, but creeping closer to their homes. This week, a judge temporarily blocked the Westlake Town Council from taking action on a development agreement for a proposed data center. Cities across the state are hitting pause on data centers and some are considering temporary moratoriums to block their development.

Some opposition to data centers is NIMBYism, but parsing through people who don’t want any new development at all, some of the public’s anxiety surrounding data centers is warranted. Texas should position itself to maintain its light-touch regulatory approach and allow business to flourish while also thinking ahead about guardrails to give residents comfort that there are protections.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Data centers represent a physical cost to the environment. They take up land that may otherwise have been used for agriculture or housing, and there are substantial energy costs. In addition to these physical manifestations, data centers are a symbol of technological intrusion into our lives and communities.

It’s understandable that people are uneasy. Communities generally know what an apartment complex or shopping center is likely to bring and what happens to these buildings as they age. They have less experience judging what a data center will mean 10 or 20 years from now and how it may impact their community.

Although they have been around for at least a decade, it wasn’t until the artificial intelligence boom that the data center industry took off. In 2013, lawmakers passed a bill creating a state sales tax exemption for data center projects, but data centers are no longer a young industry, and it’s time to reconsider these incentives.

And the Legislature should clarify whether cities can impose data center moratoriums and under what circumstances. If data centers could be prohibited because they are unpopular, what would stop cities from doing the same to other industries people view unfavorably?

Gov. Greg Abbott was right to call for a pause on data centers, and it’s time to pivot.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Texas doesn’t need to be the “epicenter” of AI as Abbott has previously championed, but it also shouldn’t be so paralyzed by fear that it drives away investment and surrenders the economic opportunities this technology can bring to the state.

A careful approach lies somewhere in the middle: require developers to bear the costs of connecting to the grid and have their own power sources, encourage industry and give communities protection too. Texas was right to pause as the consequences of the data center industry become clearer. Now lawmakers must aim to understand their impact more deeply and think beyond the next project to prepare for what comes after.

title: Octillion Power Systems Opens Third EV Battery Plant in Halol, Gujarat, India - The Buzz
description:
Octillion Power Systems has opened its third manufacturing facility in India in Halol, Gujarat.
Octillion converted the empty structure into an operational battery manufacturing plant in less than eight months.
At full capacity, the plant will produce more than 48,000 battery systems annually.
Combined with Octillion’s two existing Indian facilities, annual production in the country is expected to exceed 150,000 battery systems.
The plant also expands Octillion’s manufacturing capacity as demand for battery systems grows in India and other markets.
text:
Octillion Power Systems has opened its third manufacturing facility in India in Halol, Gujarat. The facility spans more than 13,000 square meters. Octillion converted the empty structure into an operational battery manufacturing plant in less than eight months. The facility expands the company’s production footprint in India.

At full capacity, the plant will produce more than 48,000 battery systems annually. It will provide more than 3 GWh of energy storage capacity each year.

Combined with Octillion’s two existing Indian facilities, annual production in the country is expected to exceed 150,000 battery systems. Total battery capacity is expected to reach approximately 9 GWh annually.

The facilities support passenger vehicles, trucks and light commercial vehicles, and buses.

“India is one of the most important growth markets in the global transition to electric mobility, and this facility reflects our long-term commitment to building capacity where our customers need it most,” said Paul Beach, global president of Octillion Power Systems. “Delivering a fully operational plant in under eight months is a testament to the discipline of our team and our ability to execute at speed without compromising the quality standards our customers depend on.”

Gujarat Battery Plant Opens as EV Sales Grow

The Halol facility begins operations as India’s electric vehicle market continues to expand. According to JMK Research, India’s EV sales increased 43% year over year during the first half of 2026. Sales exceeded 1.54 million units, pushing overall EV penetration above 11%.

Electric passenger car sales increased 83% year over year during the same period. Electric bus sales rose 42%.

The bus segment benefited from deployments under the government’s PM E-Bus Sewa and PM E-DRIVE programs. More than 4,200 electric buses were allocated in June. That month also recorded the highest monthly electric bus sales to date.

Electric trucks posted the highest relative growth among the segments cited. Cumulative sales increased more than 300% year over year.

Logistics, e-commerce and industrial fleets are pursuing decarbonization and total-cost-of-ownership improvements.

India aims for EVs to represent 30% of private car sales by 2030. The country also targets 70% of commercial vehicle sales and 40% of bus sales. Its target for two- and three-wheelers is 80% by 2030.

Programs supporting those targets include PM E-DRIVE and the Advanced Chemistry Cell Production-Linked Incentive scheme.

Octillion Focuses on Battery Supply Chain

Manufacturing capacity represents one part of India’s battery supply chain requirements.

India remains heavily dependent on imported lithium, cobalt and nickel for battery production. According to International Institute for Sustainable Development research, localization of several high-value components remains below 20% for many manufacturers. Those components include cells, motors and controllers.

The government’s National Critical Minerals Mission is funding domestic exploration and processing capacity. Customs duties have also been eliminated on 25 critical minerals.

A dedicated battery mineral processing policy is expected to be finalized in the coming months. The policy is intended to support a domestic value chain for battery-grade materials. Octillion said its approach to the Halol facility extends beyond battery assembly.

The plant incorporates the company’s standardized production process, thermal modeling and integrated battery management systems into the local supply base.

Octillion said the approach can reduce lead times and improve responsiveness to customers. It also adds in-country manufacturing capacity for vehicle manufacturers seeking more sourcing redundancy.

“A resilient EV supply chain in India can’t just mean more square footage — it means depth: local sourcing, local quality control, and local engineering talent working side by side with our global standards,” said Nikhil Parchure, SVP at Octillion Power Systems. “That’s what we’ve built in Halol. As India moves toward its 2030 electrification targets across cars, trucks, and buses, our customers need a partner who can scale with them without exposing them to global supply chain volatility, and that is exactly the role we intend to play.”

Halol Facility Expands Octillion Capacity

Octillion supplies EV battery packs in India for passenger vehicles, buses and commercial trucks. The Halol facility expands the company’s production capacity for India’s transportation electrification market. It also adds manufacturing redundancy and scale across Octillion’s Indian operations.

Octillion completed the facility in less than eight months. The company said the project maintained its required quality, safety and operational standards for battery production.

The plant also expands Octillion’s manufacturing capacity as demand for battery systems grows in India and other markets.

Octillion said it will continue expanding manufacturing capacity and supporting customers closer to their markets. The company also plans to continue supplying battery systems for electrified vehicles.

description:

“The Trump EPA is using every tool in the toolbox, including over $10 million in new funding, to strengthen and fortify the nation’s water workforce.
This comes at a time when water systems are working to modernize while also managing aging water infrastructure.

text:
August 19, 2026

WASHINGTON— U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is announcing the availability of $10.8 million in grant funding to support training for workers in the water sector. These essential workers play a key role in treating our nation’s drinking water and providing wastewater services that protect human health and the environment.

Enhancing recruitment and training for the water sector workforce is more important than ever in light of anticipated retirements, aging water infrastructure, evolving technologies used in the sector, and emerging risks like cyberattacks. This grant builds on the agency’s recent roundtable discussing how to help recruit and retain individuals into meaningful careers in water and to identify opportunities where EPA can help reduce barriers and improve interstate coordination.

“Every time Americans turn on the tap or flush the toilet, they depend on qualified and dedicated professionals in the water sector to ensure that drinking water is safe and wastewater is properly managed,” said EPA Assistant Administrator for Water Jess Kramer. “The Trump EPA is using every tool in the toolbox, including over $10 million in new funding, to strengthen and fortify the nation’s water workforce. We are working collaboratively with states, the water sector, and local partners to advance practical, tangible, and demonstrated effective solutions.”

Nationally, drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater systems are facing a shortage of qualified workers due to expected retirements. This comes at a time when water systems are working to modernize while also managing aging water infrastructure. Additionally, new technical and scientific skillsets are needed to prepare for new challenges like strengthening resilience to cyberattacks.

The focus of the Innovative Water Infrastructure Workforce Development Grant program is to develop a strong pool of skilled workers in the water and wastewater utilities sector. This grant program supports collaboration among federal, state, and local governments and institutions of higher education, apprentice programs, labor organizations, high schools, and other community-based organizations to provide access to workforce opportunities and build career pipelines in the water sector. The four program areas include:

Targeted internships and apprenticeships for skilled water utility trades.

Education programs designed for elementary, secondary, and higher education students.

Regional industry and workforce development collaborations to hiring qualified candidates.

Education and training programs designed for decentralized (septic) water workers to support public health for communities that rely on private wells for drinking water or septic systems.

This action makes near-term progress while the agency continues its efforts to revitalize the 2020 Water Workforce Initiative—developed and released in the first Trump Administration. Grant applications must be received by EPA through grants.gov by October 5, 2026. EPA encourages all eligible organizations who have an interest in these projects to apply.

Learn more about the Innovative Water Infrastructure Workforce Development Grant program.

title: VPP value proposition expands to affordability, reliability and resilience | Utility Dive
description:
Utilities increasingly see VPPs as affordability levers, too, said Kevin Brehm, who manages RMI’s carbon-free electricity practice.
Brehm said VPPs based around residential batteries and active managed electric vehicle charging are growing particularly fast amid slower growth in thermostat-based programs.
For utilities, well-designed VPPs can improve reliability on constrained distribution grids or provide resilience benefits in areas prone to weather-related outages or load shedding, Brehm said.
Nick Watson, director of flexible resource engineering at National Grid, said his utility is tapping distributed resource aggregations in 19 non-wires alternatives projects across its Massachusetts service territory.
ConnectedSolutions+ is an outgrowth of New England’s long-running ConnectedSolutions VPP that aggregates customer-sited resources in targeted areas of high need.
text:
Dive Brief:

Successful virtual power plants are reliable distributed resource aggregations that deliver targeted, predictable benefits for distribution or bulk power grids, a group of experts said Tuesday during a webinar organized by the Regulatory Assistance Project.

Utilities increasingly see VPPs as affordability levers, too, said Kevin Brehm, who manages RMI’s carbon-free electricity practice. On the bulk system, they can decrease power demand when wholesale prices are high and reduce both capacity and transmission costs; on distribution grids, they can free up load interconnection headroom and help reduce, defer or avoid incremental system investments, he said.

To scale customer participation in VPP programs and improve dispatchability, utilities and resource aggregators should provide robust and predictable compensation; use “revenue-grade metering” to measure performance and embed customer protections like penalty-free opt-out, said Bronte Payne, senior manager for policy at Sunrun.

Dive Insight:

VPPs are becoming more sophisticated as utilities and aggregators learn from early deployments and new resources enter the mix, said Brehm, whose team helped develop RMI’s comprehensive catalog of active U.S. VPP programs.

Brehm said VPPs based around residential batteries and active managed electric vehicle charging are growing particularly fast amid slower growth in thermostat-based programs. Multiple operational models have emerged, he added: Utility-run VPPs that compensate consumers directly or use third-party aggregators as intermediaries; “market participant” VPPs, in which resource aggregations participate directly in energy, capacity or ancillary markets; and “bring your own capacity” VPPs, an emerging model that Brehm described as a hybrid of the two.

For utilities, well-designed VPPs can improve reliability on constrained distribution grids or provide resilience benefits in areas prone to weather-related outages or load shedding, Brehm said. Consolidated Edison Co. of New York’s demand-response VPP is a good example of the former, while Puerto Rico utility Luma Energy’s Customer Battery Energy Sharing program typifies the latter, he said.

VPPs continue to evolve, with new resource models like bidirectional electric vehicle charging on the horizon, Brehm added. An analysis commissioned by General Motors last month found vehicle-to-grid integration can deliver up to 15 times more value per vehicle than one-way managed charging.

“We would love to see more vehicle-to-grid participation in VPPs … I know some of the [auto manufacturers] are beginning to advocate and get a little restless,” Brehm said.

Nick Watson, director of flexible resource engineering at National Grid, said his utility is tapping distributed resource aggregations in 19 non-wires alternatives projects across its Massachusetts service territory.

Watson said National Grid has 7.2 MW of active or committed capacity across two separate programs: ConnectedSolutions+, a residential- and small business program that leans on stationary batteries, EVs and other resources; and a more market-based front-of-meter framework for commercial and industrial customers.

ConnectedSolutions+ is an outgrowth of New England’s long-running ConnectedSolutions VPP that aggregates customer-sited resources in targeted areas of high need. In exchange for payments higher than standard ConnectedSolutions participants receive, ConnectedSolutions+ participants allow National Grid to dispatch their resources “a little bit more” and at different times of day that may reflect local demand peaks, such as Friday or Saturday evenings, Watson said.

Eversource, National Grid’s main investor-owned utility competitor in Massachusetts, has also been enrolling customers in ConnectedSolutions+.

After calculating the potential value of non-wires alternatives in constrained grid nodes, National Grid looks at factors like customer type and present ConnectedSolutions enrollment levels to determine whether ConnectedSolutions+ or the market-based framework — which requires a request for proposals process — makes more sense, Watson said.

“We screen for how much dispatchable resource we [already] have in a location,” Watson said. If the answer is ‘not much,’ an RFP may be needed.

Xcel Energy is also tapping multiple distributed resource frameworks to address emerging grid issues in Colorado, said Zach Pollock, the company’s director of grid strategy and emerging technologies.

With more than 1 GW of solar on its 7-GW Colorado system, much of it distributed on rooftops, Xcel is “starting to see some operational issues in terms of voltage swings and reverse power flow that we need to get ahead of,” he said. A corresponding reduction in the incremental value of midday solar has Xcel looking toward a “direct-participant model” that emphasizes DERs’ capacity value, he said.

“It really becomes about how do you leverage DERs not just to generate [renewable energy credits] … but really from a system perspective, how do you generate value for all the customers being asked to contribute to the cost of the grid,” Pollock said.

Xcel issued a competitive solicitation earlier this summer for the state-mandated Dispatchable Distributed Generation program, which will enroll megawatt-scale batteries “operating on a schedule to provide meaningful load reduction benefits” in areas with distribution-system constraints, Pollock said.

Pollock said Xcel has also signed up “a few megawatts” for its Active VPP program, or AVPP, which aims to enroll 25 MW of behind-the-meter resources per year for five years. Though Xcel “reserves the right” to act as its own aggregator in the future, those resources will be managed for now by third-party aggregators, he said.

title: Wood Mackenzie predicts that global energy insecurity could cause EV surge
description:
Supporting the scenario To anticipate the resulting increased demand for EV charging, Wood Mackenzie suggested that countries could need to focus on managed charging.
Wood Mackenzie additionally estimated that a $45 billion investment in greenfield metal supply would comfortably support the heightened EV growth demonstrated in the electric shock scenario.
In its electric shock scenario, Wood Mackenzie predicted that tariff relief could encourage Chinese investment in local manufacturing, which would both protect jobs and progress Europe’s EV transition.
Investing in EVs Under the electric shock scenario, EV infrastructure growth would be driven by a sharp incline in customer demand.
Wood Mackenzie noted that 7 million EV chargers have a 15% utilisation rate.
text:
Research and consultancy group Wood Mackenzie has revealed findings from its recent ‘Horizons’ report, which predicts that EVs will increase from 4% of the global fleet to 25% by 2040.

Titled ‘Electric shock: How electric vehicles could hit the accelerator’, the report assesses how the impact of oil prices, policies in favour of EVs, and technological advancement could progress EV adoption.

Three factors that could support the EV transition have been identified, which the firm highlights in its ‘electric shock’ scenario:

David Brown, director of energy transition research at Wood Mackenzie, commented on the findings: “If these forces converge all at once, the effect on EV adoption could be dramatic.”

"Our electric shock scenario models what happens when policy, consumer behaviour and technology all move in the same direction, quantifying the implications for commodities and power markets."

The scenario predicted that global oil demand could fall to 99 million barrels per day (mb/d) by 2040, which would be 5 mb/d below the base case. This could then lead to the closure of 40 oil refineries across the world.

Supporting the scenario

To anticipate the resulting increased demand for EV charging, Wood Mackenzie suggested that countries could need to focus on managed charging. By moving charging to times where grid supply is high, and costs are low – as is the case with 50% of European charging – grids would be kept stable and costs competitive.

Wood Mackenzie additionally estimated that a $45 billion investment in greenfield metal supply would comfortably support the heightened EV growth demonstrated in the electric shock scenario.

Copper mining would require a $25 billion investment, as mine capacity would need to increase from 850,000 tonnes per year to around 960,000 by 2040. However, capital would then be directed to “higher risk” areas, and China could gain a firmer foothold if mining regions in the Americas failed to remain competitive.

As such, the firm identified copper as “the most critical bottleneck” in supporting the metal supply.

International findings

Wood Mackenzie’s report found that China was leading the way with EV car sales. In Q2 2026, EVs accounted for 42% of Chinese car sales – an increase from last year’s figure of 33%. The report predicted that China’s new restrictions on gasoline consumption, full purchase tax exemptions, and larger purchase credits could combine with electric shock to further the country’s EV transition.

Overall, annual sales could increase from 8.9 million in 2025 to 29.9 million in 2040, and manufacturing capacity could grow in 2035 by 50%.

When assessing the United States, Wood Mackenzie’s described its contrast with China as “stark”. If the country did not invest in advanced battery technologies and competitive supply chains, the firm warned that the nation may lose its domestic market to international competitors.

Passenger EV sales in the US were down by 33% in H1 of 2026 from the same period in 2025, due to the government’s withdrawal of tax incentives. EVs currently account for 3% of the US’ vehicle fleet.

The report hypothesised that the electric shock scenario could combine with a suggested policy that attracts foreign investment into the US’ EV market, making the US EV fleet 51% larger than its base case by 2040.

Europe, by contrast, has “strong decarbonisation ambitions but significant headwinds” as its auto sector saw layoffs of around 60,000. In its electric shock scenario, Wood Mackenzie predicted that tariff relief could encourage Chinese investment in local manufacturing, which would both protect jobs and progress Europe’s EV transition.

Investing in EVs

Under the electric shock scenario, EV infrastructure growth would be driven by a sharp incline in customer demand.

Wood Mackenzie noted that 7 million EV chargers have a 15% utilisation rate. Its electric shock scenario would quickly increase this, and the demand would prompt countries to install more ports.

China would need to invest around $200 billion incrementally, and Europe would need $108 billion to construct 2.7 million new ports.

“Geopolitics, consumer behaviour and technological innovation could converge to lift EV sales faster than in our base case,” added Brown.

“For OECD countries, securing critical mineral supplies and technological know-how over time will deliver lasting strategic advantage.”
